#4897. The 94 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 11 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4896. Scheduling Your Day Like This May Reduce Physical Pain and Lessen Depression

Here’s why your body and brain love this.

It can be hard to think of anything else when you’re dealing with physical pain and depression. Though treatments for each are very different, new research suggests that a simple lifestyle trick might help ease symptoms of each: Keeping a consistent schedule.

A recent study published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine makes a solid case for having a routine and dealing with less physical and mental pain. Researchers specifically found that older adults who follow a regular daily schedule tend to have less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they have insomnia.

The findings shouldn’t be interpreted to mean putting yourself on a schedule will magically make your pain and depression disappear. Instead, it suggests that having a daily routine could be a complement to the treatments you’re already doing, like physical therapy, talk therapy, and taking an antidepressant. Here’s what doctors recommend keeping in mind—and why they’re on board with the idea of creating and sticking with a regular schedule.

Meet the experts: Eunjin L. Tracy, PhD, lead study author and director of the Sleep, Health, and Relationships Lab at the University of Missouri; Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and the author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It; and Beth Malow, MD, a neurologist and chief of the Division of Sleep Disorders at Vanderbilt Health.

For the study, researchers surveyed 67 older adults—37 of those had insomnia and 30 said they slept well. People who said they experienced insomnia were also likely to report that they had more physical pain and higher levels of depression than those who didn’t have insomnia.

But when the researchers dug deeper, they also discovered that participants who stuck with consistent daily schedules reported less pain and fewer symptoms of depression, whether they struggled with insomnia or not.

“The results suggest that greater behavioral-social rhythm regularity is associated with more favorable health outcomes,” the researchers wrote in the study.

The study simply found an association, so it didn’t prove that sticking with a consistent schedule leads to less pain and depression. But experts say there’s likely something here.

“Regular daily routines help keep the body's internal clock synchronized, and that clock influences many systems tied to mood, pain sensitivity, and metabolism,” says Eunjin L. Tracy, PhD, lead study author and director of the Sleep, Health, and Relationships Lab at the University of Missouri.

A consistent schedule can also help support your nervous system, according to Beth Malow, MD, a neurologist and chief of the Division of Sleep Disorders at Vanderbilt Health. “There are many chemicals that are released into our nervous systems during the day and night,” she says. “When we have a consistent schedule, our brains and bodies are more responsive to these chemicals—think of it similarly to taking a prescription medication at the same time every day.” That can lead to less physical pain and a better mood, Dr. Malow says.

An inconsistent schedule can also interfere with activities that tend to combat depression and pain, like exercise, says Christopher Winter, MD, a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and the author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It.

“It's also possible that other factors, such as personality traits like conscientiousness, contribute both to more regular routines and to better health,” Dr. Tracy says.

Ultimately, doctors say more research is needed. “This is a [well] known relationship, although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood,” Dr. Winter says.

A schedule only works if it’s one you’ll actually follow. Dr. Winter recommends starting with a consistent wake time. “This tends to lend itself to a routine at least with breakfast and coffee, and helps with bedtime,” he says. Try to be consistent with that bedtime, too, adds Dr. Malow. “Even meals can affect our schedule,” she says. “Try to eat at similar times of the day to promote consistency.”

Dr. Winter calls exercise “a daily requirement,” adding that it should be outside if possible to get exposure to sunlight. And, if you can schedule this at a consistent time in your day, even better.

“You don't need to change everything at once,” Dr. Tracy says. “Start with one anchor, keep it consistent, and build from there.”

#4895. What Is Self-Custody? How to Hold Your Own Crypto Keys

What Is Self-Custody? How to Hold Your Own Crypto Keys

When you buy crypto on an exchange, the exchange usually holds it for you. Your account shows a balance, but the private keys that control the coins belong to the trading platform.

The risk is that if an exchange collapses, is hacked or freezes withdrawals, its customers can lose access to their funds. The collapse of FTX in November 2022 left millions of users unable to withdraw, and turned the old crypto saying "not your keys, not your coins" into a rallying cry.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Self-custody is the alternative: holding your crypto yourself, with no intermediary standing between you and your money. This guide explains what self-custody is, how it works, the tools available and the risks it brings.

Self-custody means you, and only you, control the private keys to your crypto.

On a blockchain, coins are not stored in a wallet in the way cash sits in a purse. They are recorded on a public ledger, and a private key, a long secret number, is what proves you have the right to spend them. Whoever holds the private key controls the coins.

With a custodial service, such as a centralized exchange, the company holds the keys on your behalf, and you rely on it to process your withdrawals. With a self-custodial, or non-custodial, wallet, the keys are generated and stored on your own device, and transactions only happen when you approve them.

When you set up a self-custodial wallet, it generates a seed phrase, usually a list of 12 or 24 words. The seed phrase is a human-readable backup of your private keys: anyone who has it can recreate your wallet on another device and move your funds.

That makes the seed phrase the single most important thing to protect. Most guides recommend writing it down on paper or stamping it into metal, storing it somewhere safe offline, and never typing it into a website, sharing it or saving it in a photo or cloud file.

Self-custodial wallets come in several forms:

Custodial services are easier to use. If you forget your password, you can reset it, and an exchange handles the security of its own systems. But you are trusting the company to stay solvent, keep your funds safe and let you withdraw when you want to.

Self-custody removes that counterparty risk, and means no company can freeze your funds or block a transaction. The tradeoff is responsibility: there is no password reset. If you lose your seed phrase, or someone steals it, there is usually no way to get your crypto back.

Welshman James Howells says the keys to about 8,000 BTC are on a hard drive that was thrown out in 2013 and buried in a landfill in Newport, Wales.

Losing your keys is the most common risk, but not the only one.

Hardware can have flaws. In July 2026, a firmware vulnerability in Coldcard, a Bitcoin-only air-gapped hardware wallet, let attackers reconstruct some users' seed phrases. Losses rose to nearly $114 million in Bitcoin within days, according to Galaxy Research. Even the most secure devices depend on their makers getting the code right.

Phishing and malware are a constant threat to software wallets, and scammers often pose as wallet support staff to trick users into handing over seed phrases.

Holders also face physical danger. So-called "wrench attacks," in which criminals use violence to force victims to hand over crypto, have surged. Blockchain security firm CertiK verified 52 wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up from 39 a year earlier, and Chainalysis said such attacks were on pace for a record year.

The threat is one reason holders have pushed back against proposals to make them report large self-custody holdings to tax authorities, warning that such records could leak.

Moving crypto off an exchange generally involves a few steps:

Regulators have long debated how to handle self-custodial, or "unhosted," wallets. In October 2026, the U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network withdrew a 2020 proposal that would have required banks and money services businesses to keep records on transactions with self-custodial wallets over $3,000 and report those over $10,000.

In France, the Senate rejected a plan in November 2026 that would have required holders to declare self-custodied crypto worth more than €100,000.

Self-custody is starting to extend beyond humans. In 2026, MetaMask launched Agent Wallet, a self-custodial wallet that lets AI agents execute on-chain trades within limits set by the user, while Coinbase introduced its own self-custodial wallets for AI agents.

Wallet makers are also working to make self-custody easier for newcomers, with features such as social logins and passkeys that reduce reliance on seed phrases. But the core principle remains the same: whoever controls the keys controls the crypto.

#4894. In Khalil Mack's Los Angeles Penthouse, the Ceiling Glows and the Kids Climb the Walls

Brianna Mack is outnumbered. Her husband is the NFL linebacker Khalil Mack. Their sons, Deuce and Kylo, five and four, run around like the Marvel characters they love. Still, walk through their Los Angeles penthouse and you see Brianna everywhere. The mohair rugs are soft, if not precious, because she wanted the kids to be able to roll around on them. A fluted marble fireplace and a Ferrari Sheppard painting make visitors stop and stare. “That piece looks like Brianna,” says AD PRO Directory interior designer Ryan Saghian. “The confidence, the way the figure is sitting back. She’s got swag. It was made for her.” Brianna built the room around it. “Nice, soft, but not overly feminine,” Brianna says of the balance she struck. “I think that’s life when you’re the only female among three males.”

Khalil with his son on the De Sede sofa. Coffee table by Eternity Modern.

“It’s like a stop-and-think piece,” Brianna Mack says of the Ferrari Sheppard artwork that anchors the entry. Rick Owens ebony stool; marble console by Coco Republic; Ferm Living rug; walls in Portola Roman Clay. Art advisor: Jenna Cesolini.

They were previously living in Newport, California. Khalil was losing four hours a day commuting to the LA Chargers’ facility in El Segundo. Now he’s fifteen minutes from work. Thirty on a day of bad traffic. But Brianna worried about what her sons would sacrifice. Their new home would have no backyard space. “Before we even knew the colors, before we picked out any materials, we knew that was going to be a priority,” she says. The solution: a soundproof playroom with a climbing wall, designed so the boys could be their cherished Marvel characters without disturbing the neighbors below. “We never want to restrain them from being who they are,” Brianna says.

“It’s like their own little mansion in the sky,” Ryan Saghian says. De Sede sofa; armchairs by Amber Lewis for Four Hands; vintage Moroccan rug; antique Dutch library table from Chak Monet Antiques; dried manzanita from Potting Hill; drapery in Fabricut.

The Mack family in the living room. De Sede sofa; walls in Portola Roman Clay.

The Hermès plates were collected from Lapérouse in Paris, a Mack family tradition when traveling. Table and chairs by Eichholtz Los Angeles; chair upholstery by Innovations; pendant by Veneto Luce.

Shearling armchair and ottoman by Amber Lewis for Four Hands; coffee tables by Eternity Modern; rug from Caravan Rugs; drapery in Fabricut; walls in Portola Roman Clay.

The couple hired Saghian, a 34-year-old designer whose clientele runs heavy on athletes and entertainers. He describes Brianna as “the opposite of basic.” His challenge was honoring that without overwhelming Khalil’s minimalism. “The high-fashion elements that are more related to her aesthetic, I introduced in places like artwork, the rugs,” he says. “But the overall architecture of the space I kept as minimal as I possibly could.” Due to his busy schedule, Khalil was often absent during the design process. “He wasn’t in the meetings,” Brianna says, but she knew his taste as well as her own. Saghian, she says, “just got it.” The project, which took two years, involved gutting the place to the studs, starting over with Roman clay walls and hardware-free cabinetry. Touch latches. Finger pulls. Nothing to interrupt the quiet they were seeking.

“No moldings, it’s all Roman clay,” Ryan Saghian says of the walls throughout. A sepia-toned landscape mural by Belarte Studio wraps the formal dining room. Table and chairs by Eichholtz Los Angeles; plaster relief sculpture by Uttermost; Veneto Luce pendant.

While the family has a private chef, Khalil still enjoys cooking for his family. Here, the NFL star prepares a meal while Brianna and their sons gather at the island. Cabinetry by Gefen Builders; Wolf appliances; natural quartzite countertops.

The kitchen’s waterfall-edge quartzite island was chosen after the couple visited stone yards in person. Cognac leather stools with brass bases; cabinetry by Gefen Builders; pendant by Apparatus Studio.

On Khalil’s days off, he cooks breakfast. The boys eat at a round dining table with a shattered-glass finish, leather bar stools in cognac around it. A wall of plates from memorable restaurants they’ve visited, Lapérouse in Paris among them. The kitchen was designed to be durable. Two young sons and an NFL player’s appetite will test any surface. But when morning light fills the room, Brianna takes it in. “This is beautiful,” she says. “This is our space.”

“When you’re looking at these beautiful textures, it does affect your mood,” Brianna Mack says. A Monica Ord painting hangs above a travertine pedestal in the hallway; walls throughout are finished in Portola Roman Clay.

“It just has this zen to it,” Brianna Mack says of the home’s atmosphere. The powder room’s custom stone vanity is carved from a single slab; walls in Portola Roman Clay; backlit mirror.

“He loves his wife—I mean, he’s obsessed with her—and he loves his kids. I’ve never seen a guy like that,” Ryan Saghian says. Brianna Mack with Deuce and Kylo in the primary suite’s sitting area. Sofa by J.Alexander Furniture; artwork by William McLure; Moroccan alpaca-mohair rug from Caravan Rugs.

The primary suite’s sitting area. Sofa by J.Alexander Furniture in S.Harris fabric; swivel chairs and coffee table by Eichholtz Los Angeles; pendant by Vakkerlight in alabaster and saddle leather; Moroccan alpaca-mohair rug from Caravan Rugs; artwork by William McLure; florals by Goodroots LA.

“This is a guy who comes home exhausted not only mentally but physically,” Saghian says of Khalil. So they knocked down walls and rebuilt what was necessary: hyperbaric chamber, massage space. “I needed a spot like this to just relax and recover,” Khalil says. Brianna took a room nearby for hair and makeup. And when the work is done, there’s a screening room that includes a pit-style sofa, a candy bar, and a glowing fiber-optic ceiling. Saghian borrowed the last detail from a Rolls-Royce. “I look at [game] film in there if I need to,” Khalil says. “But it’s more fun to watch movies as a family there.”

A black marble soaking tub, so heavy it required building approval before it could enter the elevator, sits between dual rain showers. Checkerboard floor in black and cream marble.

The primary bath’s checkerboard floor in black and cream marble anchors a floating travertine vanity. Cabinetry by Gefen Builders.

A sculptural travertine lounger curves beneath an arched niche in the primary bath’s steam room.

The playroom was a priority from the first meeting. Beneath the cork and rubber underlayment is half an inch of soundproofing. Build-out by Gefen Builders; padded walls and drapery in Fabricut; pendant by Vakkerlight.

"They love to be Spider-Man climbing,” Brianna Mack says. The playroom was converted from a guest room, with soundproof walls and a half-inch rubber layer beneath the hardwood. Build-out by Gefen Builders; padded walls by Phillip Jeffries; drapery in Fabricut; pendant by Vakkerlight.

In the boy’s bedroom, the bed wall is entirely custom, with twin beds set into niches and recessed shelves; footballs from their father line the opposite wall. Bedding by Parachute; chest by Pottery Barn; rug by Nordik Knots.

“We really own this space,” Brianna says. “A place for our boys to feel loved and to have a sense of identity.” She had hoped for something good. She got more than that. “It superseded what I thought it would be.” Some mornings, before the noise starts, just as the light begins to fill their home, she looks around and takes it in. “I’m falling more in love with the space,” Brianna says. A life they built from the studs up.

“It’s basically one huge wall-to-wall pit that the whole family can get on to watch TV,” Ryan Saghian says. The room, converted from the den, features padded walls by Phillip Jeffries; motorized drapery in Fabricut; custom modular seating; and a fiber-optic ceiling inspired by a Rolls-Royce.

Former FTX chief operating officer Constance Waing has slammed Netflix’s portrayal of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao in The Altruists as racist, saying it relied on Asian mafia stereotypes.

Woke 1 may have been crazy, but racist is still racist says Vitalik Buterin.

South Korean crypto exchanges Upbit and Bithumb suspended deposits and withdrawals of CYBER on Sunday after the project reported suspicious activity involving its cross-chain bridge.

On Saturday, Cyber said it detected unexpected minting of CYBER tokens on Solana, followed by a transfer of tokens out of its bridge’s Ethereum lockbox. Cyber, formerly CyberConnect, operates an Ethereum layer-2 network designed for social applications.

The project said it was investigating the incident and advised users to avoid using the bridge or depositing CYBER to exchanges while the investigation continues.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) unveiled a draft bill Tuesday that would initially limit issuance of won-denominated stablecoins to groups majority-owned by banks and generally cap shareholders’ stakes in crypto exchanges at 20%.

The draft also seeks to lift South Korea’s 2017 ban on domestic initial coin offerings.

The 20% ownership rule is set to affect a deal that Naver struck for Upbit owner Dunamu. The deal gave Naver full control, but under the new rules shares above the 20% cap would lose their vote.

South Korean fintech companies could gain influence in bank-led stablecoin groups by signing up partners that help people spend won-denominated tokens, Tiger Research said in its Tuesday report.

“Those relationships are likely to matter more to the business than the volume of stablecoins issued,” the Asia-focused research company said.

The US Department of Justice is seeking to recover more than $1.1 billion in crypto stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance in October by North Korean hackers.

In a court filing Monday, prosecutors asked a federal court in Washington, DC, to permanently forfeit the funds, which are held in the USDC stablecoin. Since the attack, US authorities said they have helped to freeze, seize or return nearly $3 billion of the more than $6 billion taken from Binance.

Japanese financial giants SBI Holdings and Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMFG) have launched a joint venture with the Solana Foundation to tokenize assets, develop stablecoin payment infrastructure and expand onchain financial services across Asia.

Japan’s Financial Services Agency has published briefing materials considering proposals to regulate apps and sites that connect to DeFi, and whether to discourage access to protocols that lack money laundering controls.

Daiwa has completed a technical verification in which AI agents processed natural language instructions to screen various DEX options and to conduct stablecoin and security token swaps.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) launched a platform Wednesday that supports round-the-clock settlement of tokenized debt securities in multiple currencies.

The CMU Digital Asset Platform, developed and operated by CMU OmniClear Limited on behalf of the HKMA, uses cash tokens for payment and connects with conventional payment systems and central bank digital currencies.

Hong Kong has published a bill that would bring crypto custodians, advisers and other virtual asset service providers under mandatory licensing or registration.

On Friday, the government officially published its Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026, proposing that firms carrying out those activities would need to obtain a license from, or register with, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). The bill is set for its first reading in the Legislative Council on Dec. 2.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore has clarified that an on-chain token is not automatically a bank deposit. It draws a line between genuine tokenized deposits and crypto-like bearer instruments.

A UK court has approved an asset recovery settlement totaling 55 million pounds from Su Haijin and Xu Haika, two defendants in Singapore’s largest money-laundering case. Haika is being forced to sell 16 London apartments held through affiliated companies to repay the funds. The August 2023 police operation saw crypto worth more than S$38 million seized.

According to Nikkei Asia, Bitmart has a $319.5 million shortfall but just $1.9 million in liquid assets available for customer repayments. Numerous users report they have been unable to access their accounts.Bitmart disclosed the figures to Alvarez & Marsal, which is overseeing the restructuring process. The collapse highlights the dangers of high yield crypto products, with Chinese investors reportedly drawn to the platform by short term savings products offering 18.8% annualized yields for 14 day deposits.

#4891. The 61 Best New Shows of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

We've got murder mysteries, stories of love and lust, and lots and lots of Yellowstone. And that's just the beginning.

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock)

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix)

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

#4890. Vibecoded GTA 6 PC Ports Are Now Rendering In-Game Graphics Despite Take-Two Crackdown

Vibecoded GTA 6 PC Ports Are Now Rendering In-Game Graphics Despite Take-Two Crackdown

It took Rockstar Games more than a decade to develop Grand Theft Auto 6. It took a bunch of anonymous vibe coders less than a week to get parts of it running on a platform Rockstar hasn't released it for.

Unofficial PC ports of GTA 6 are now capable of rendering in-game graphics and handling player inputs, according to footage circulating on social media. Some projects have achieved speeds of around 20 frames per second, despite the increasingly aggressive efforts of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive to shut them down.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

A developer going by AvatarManz reportedly achieved between six and 20 frames per second using an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX, a high-end graphics card. The unofficial port consumed up to 46 GB of system memory, considerably more than what a typical gaming PC has available.

Another demonstration reported Thursday appears to show a character riding a jet ski and driving along the coast at between 19 and 23 frames per second. Performance drops to around 12 frames per second in urban areas, and patches of water are visibly missing from the scene.

new GTA 6 PC gameplay shows walking around the prologue, with textures, lighting and physics looking much better. Ray tracing is reportedly working too.

Still only 1–3fps on an RTX 5070 Ti, Ryzen 7 7800X3D and 32GB DDR5. Visuals are coming along, performance has a way to go. pic.twitter.com/ON00pzHFHX

According to community tracking data site Portwatch VI, at least six of 35 tracked projects have reportedly reached interactive gameplay. Some developers have also managed to get ray tracing working, a computationally demanding technique that simulates how light interacts with objects.

The footage and performance figures have not been independently verified, and none of the projects has demonstrated that the entire game can be played reliably on a PC.

Much of the progress comes from developers relying on vibe coding, a method of software development in which users instruct AI models to generate and debug code using natural language rather than manually writing every instruction.

The developers aren't recreating GTA 6 from scratch. They're reverse-engineering an existing Xbox build and developing software that allows its code to execute on Windows, translating console-specific instructions and accommodating differences in how PCs handle graphics and other hardware functions.

AI coding tools such as Anthropic's Claude have dramatically accelerated this kind of work, reducing some tasks that previously took months to days. Optimizing the resulting software and fixing the inevitable bugs are separate challenges, especially for a game as complex as GTA 6.

And the whole thing, of course, spaked a meme coin.

As Decrypt previously reported, notorious Rockstar leaker Cyberleek distributed what they claimed was a 209 GB Xbox build of GTA 6, withholding its main executable file as part of an attempt to push their CYBERLEEK meme coin to a $15 million market capitalization.

The token failed to reach its target, but Cyberleek released the executable on November 23 anyway. Within a day, some of the most prominent porting projects, including Leonida and GTA6Modding, went dark.

Take-Two subsequently confirmed its involvement through a copyright complaint targeting Leonida. GitHub disabled 3,007 repositories associated with the project.

In its DMCA notice, Take-Two argued that the project reproduces copyrighted material and violates Rockstar's terms of service, which prohibit unauthorized reverse engineering and decompilation.

Some developers have since taken their work into private communities, making their progress harder to independently assess.

Rockstar released GTA 6 on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, targeting 30 frames per second on consoles. It has yet to announce a release date for an official PC version.

#4889. This Historic Home Is Built Around a Spectacular Light Well That Looks Like a Connect Four Game

Long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets. Washerwomen and their families lived in narrow, two-story houses, and the women would go to the wells every day to hand-wash clothes. It is in this unique part of the city that you’ll find one of architect Raúl Sánchez’s latest projects.

The lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building. From here, you can see the living area, a corner of the kitchen island, the bottom of the blue light well, and the white-painted beams. Santina chairs from the 1970s are by Carlo Sant.

“It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes. We were asked to restore it for a couple and their child,” explains Sánchez. The house faces two streets: Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers. Since there’s a five-foot difference in the elevation of the two streets, Sánchez decided to add a landing at the higher entrance off Granollers, where one flight of stairs descends to a lower level, which opens onto Calle Aiguafreda, and the other ascends to the upper level of the small house, where the bedrooms and a bathroom are located.

In the living room, the floor is made of terra-cotta tiles that echo the traditional clay paving in the home’s garden. A rectangular skylight is offset by 45 degrees from the rest of the room and lacquered in a deep blue, which is complemented by a red reading corner with a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer (Knoll), and a yellow folding screen. Between two Amanta armchairs by Mario Bellini (Hay) there’s an Altar side table by Ewe Studio (Tacchini). In front of them is a C cork stool designed by Jasper Morrison (Vitra). Atollo lamp by Vico Magistretti (Oluce).

Sánchez added a new architectural element: a light well that extends from a skylight on the roof through the full height of the building, illuminating even the ground-floor spaces, some of which are partially below street level. Pierced by a series of circular openings, like a Connect 4 game, and coated in a glossy blue lacquer, the light shaft evokes an ancient well while also serving as a contemporary, poetic, and functional architectural element.

Halfway up the ground floor, the house has a second entrance from the street. Sánchez added a landing there with two flights of steps: one leading down to the living area, the other leading up to the bedrooms and the bathroom.

A light well topped with a skylight runs the full height of the building, illuminating the spaces all the way down to the ground floor. The 45-degree rotation relative to the rest of the structure defines the home’s circulation and breaks up any feeling of predictable regularity. Perforated with circular openings and coated in blue lacquer, it gives the home a spectacular architectural feature.

It also stands out as an organizing feature of the home, thanks to its 45-degree rotation relative to the floor plan. “This rotated geometry allows for the dynamic opening and closing of different perspectives and circulation paths, thereby avoiding a predictable corridor-like effect,” says Sánchez. “The circular openings also allow for views between rooms and across different levels.” Cut into all four sides of the light well, the circles allow natural light to enter from the skylight on the roof. As the sunlight moves across the walls of the light well throughout the day, the spectacular blue lacquer comes to life.

A large, custom-designed installation by Raúl Sánchez Architects runs from the kitchen to the living room, organizing and defining the spaces. Most of it matches the color of the walls, but it transitions from pale-yellow cabinets in the kitchen to lacquered wood in the living room. Ceramic pieces by Catalina Montaña (@hellobigmontana).

A stone countertop with subtle yellow veining plays off the chick-yellow fronts of the kitchen cabinets. The 9091 kettle is by Richard Sapper (Alessi). Skan pendant light (Vibia).

At the foot of the staircase leading to Calle Granollers, the mirrored door to the bathroom offers a unique perspective on the living area and the skylight.

The first floor, which is a compact 431 square feet, is designed as an open space with living and dining areas, a small office, and a kitchen. At its center is the deep-blue light well, a graphic element that punctuates the mostly neutral color scheme. A folding screen made of wood and rice paper is a special feature for one of the owners, who once lived in Japan; it can either connect or separate the office from the living area. A small powder room is positioned at a 45-degree angle so the door can’t be seen from the main living area. Near the Aiguafreda entrance, a kitchen island, also placed on a diagonal, is clad in mirrors, helping to create a sense of lightness and maintaining the open feeling and flow of the space.

A view of the living area from the small office. White and terra-cotta dominate, accented by splashes of color. In the foreground is a Kyoto table by Gianfranco Frattini (Poltrona Frau).

The house is rooted in the history of both its neighborhood and the specific alley where it is located, and the chosen materials engage in a dialogue with the past. On the first floor, terra-cotta tiles echo the traditional clay paving found in the home’s outdoor space. Colorful glazed tiles adorn the sinks and bathroom walls, with reddish-tone lacquers and paints recalling the clay soil long found in nearby orchards. The glossy blue color and circular perforations of the skylight elicit water droplets from a washing well.

The light filtering through the circular openings of the blue light well casts a glow on the vanity, which is partially clad in red ceramic tiles that cover the countertop and extend up to the ceiling.

The Dioscuri wall sconces (Artemide) blend right in with the play of colors and both the round and rectangular shapes in the hallway leading to the bathroom.

“The mirror-like surfaces of the doors and the kitchen island, with their slight distortions, evoke the reflections on the surface of the water,” says Sánchez. “Above all, the renovation has made it possible to preserve all the elements that give the home its character and history while also integrating contemporary, energy-efficient systems.”

The light well, painted entirely in blue, is at once architectural, functional, and playful.

The home’s green installations include an aerothermal system for air-conditioning, heating, and hot water; a new floor slab on the first floor to limit indoor humidity; enhanced thermal insulation in the roof; and improvements to the thermal and acoustic performance of the façades and shared walls. In addition, the skylight opens to take advantage of a thermal stack effect, expelling hot air in the summer while capturing heat in the winter–transforming the project’s central design element into a system that is both functional and contributes to the home’s environmental sustainability. The interior renovation is only the first phase of the project: Sánchez is currently redesigning the narrow garden, a plot that’s 13 feet wide by 98 feet long.

This home tour was first published by Architectural Digest Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

In the child‘s room, primary colors and a 1980s vibe dominate. The Veronica chair is by Afra and Tobia Scarpa (Casas). The AJ lamp is by Arne Jacobsen (Louis Poulsen).

A view into the light well, which provides illumination and ventilation.

A view of the hallway and staircase from the primary bedroom, whose entryway is painted red, setting the stage for the entrance into the room. Extra-large, veined-wood cabinet handles adorn the full-height cabinet fronts. In the foreground, a Reno chair by Federico Correa and Alfonso Milá from 1961. The Dioscuri wall sconce is by Artemide.

The primary bedroom, located under the roof, is bathed in light. The custom built-in storage units (Raúl Sánchez Architects) feature a stepped design, and the spectacular wood handles, with their prominent grain, add a circular geometric pattern to the space.

The house’s arbor gives it a rural charm, especially surprising given its location in the heart of Barcelona.

#4888. Which LED Face Mask Is the Best Buy on Black Friday? Take Up to 59% Off These Expert-Tested Devices

You can also save big on red light therapy tools for hair growth from HairMax, iRestore, and Celluma.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Black Friday is packed with major discounts on dermatologist-recommended, editor-tested red light therapy tools, including LED face masks. I’ve been all in on red light therapy since 2018 after my esthetician introduced me to the Women’s Health Skincare Award-winning brand Celluma. Whenever I use my array of red light therapy tools, I’ve noticed my face is more luminous, even-toned, and youthful-looking. When I take extended pauses, my skin looks dull and my breakouts become more frequent. While these devices start around $300 and can easily cost half my rent, Black Friday is an opportune time to shop and save up to 59 percent off editor-tested devices.

So what exactly makes LED face masks so effective? They’re equipped with light-emitting diodes (LEDs) that emit various wavelengths and colors. My personal favorites are red and near-infrared wavelengths that boost skin radiance and address my stubborn smile lines. Some masks, such as the Ulike, are equipped with blue wavelengths to help target acne-causing bacteria. It’s a must-have for my oily, acne-prone skin. You might also find it helpful if you’re going through surprising skin changes in your 40s, which include acne.

To help you discover my most-trusted devices, I combed the Web for the Black Friday LED face mask deals. I also found impressive sales on more niche red light therapy tools, such as an iRestore LED neck and chest mask and devices that help promote hair growth. Given the fast-paced, fleeting nature of Black Friday deals, I’ll be updating this story frequently throughout the big day, so be sure to bookmark this page for the most accurate sales information. But don’t delay too long—many of these deals will disappear after midnight PT.

#4887. These Are the 46 Best Action Movies Ever Made

AS LONG AS there are movies, there will be action movies. Why? Because no young girl or boy grows up pretending to be a damsel in distress or a sidekick. They all want to punch, draw swords, and run toward the danger. They are the heroes and the future directors, choreographers, and performers who bring these imaginations to life.

And to the incredulity of your father (who insists no movie will ever top First Blood) the action genre hasn’t slipped on it’s roundhouse kick. If anything, we are now experiencing another golden age of ass-kicking cinema. While there are obvious developments in VFX technology, which have allowed for larger set pieces and more realistic thrills, much of what makes a great acton film a great action film hasn’t changed: painstaking choreography, fearless stunt performers/actors, and clear cinematography (and not that Taken fence jumping bullshit.)

The only thing that’s changed are the names and faces. Legend action directors like Ang Lee, John Woo, Robert Clouse, and Zhang Yimou (still going strong) have given way to newer arrivals like Gareth Evans, Chad Stahelski, and Christopher Nolan. And performers like Bruce Lee, Jean-Claude Van Damme, and Arnold have changed to Tony Jaa, Iko Uwais, and Charlize Theron.

If anything, the fights are becoming more brutal, more carefully choreographed, and more ambitious. And international actors and directors are finally getting increased attention (and direction) in a Hollywood overly-saturated with slapstick cinematography and post-production punches.

Here’s hoping for more John Wicks, more Raids, and more Atomic Blondes in the future. Until then, here is, in no particular order, the 36 best action movies ever made.

John Rambo would become increasingly cartoonish as the sequels went on, but in the original, he was just a scared veteran trying to survive out in the real world.

The Raid was more frenzied, but the sequel (also written and directed by Gareth Evans) got grand, introducing an intricate crime-drama plot. Didn’t matter: Redemption is brilliantly violent, a ballet of broken bones, perfect punches and crazy car chases.

The film marked the breakout moment for Muy Thai martial artist Tony Jaa and the beginning of one of the best action franchises ever. There’s not a lot of fakery in Jaa’s fight scenes. Dudes are getting punched for real.

The second film is more dialogue-heavy, but the first half is essentially nonstop action … and it’s a good thing the Crazy 88 fight is in black and white, because it’d almost be too bloody to watch otherwise.

What should have been Jason Bourne’s final adventure is a thrilling, satisfying conclusion to this kinetic trilogy. Director Paul Greengrass and star Matt Damon permanently reshaped how we think of the globetrotting espionage thriller. James Bond is still playing catch-up.

Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation (2015)

You can’t go wrong with any in this series – though it has only gotten better as the years have gone along – but the introduction of Rebecca Ferguson to this series just amped up the emotional stakes.

Keanu Reeves’ first of two masterful franchises on this list, John Wick gave us a mournful 21st-century assassin who won’t let his grief get in the way of shooting every bad guy in the head at point-blank range.

Bruce Lee was popular before this film, but this is what sent him into the stratosphere. Well-made from start to finish, and absolutely unrelenting. The best part about it is that there isn’t a gun to be found in the whole film.

Ong-Bak gave us Tony Jaa and Muy Thai, and Ip Man gave us Donnie Yen and Wing Chun. While Yen had been in many other great action films previously (check out Kill Zone — S.P.L.), its the Ip Man films that will define his legacy, the character forever his—the semi-biographical person of Ip Man, Bruce Lee’s trainer. Though the films can feel a bit jingoistic at times (they’re basically Hong Kong’s Rambo), the fight scenes are femur-breaking legendary.

Zhang Yimou’s magnum opus, Daggers is maybe more love story than a martial arts film—and so the most action-packed love story of all time—but “love story” is no cinematic pejorative. The film features the most colorful and vibrant cinematography of any film on this list. Action is a visual genre. And no film here is more pleasing to the eyes.

John Woo’s Hollywood career wasn’t as sparkling or consistent as fans would have hoped, but this late-‘80s peak remains a glorious salute to melodramatic plotting and poetic shootouts. Chow Yun-fat made for a fierce, soulful assassin — and, never forget, The Killer is where Woo began his obsession with dove-filled action scenes, which have been parodied everywhere from 21 Jump Street to Scary Movie 2.

Oh, don’t dare not think of this as an action movie. The existential dread of Ridley Scott’s original is replaced by James Cameron’s trademark intensity, and even though this has aliens and spaceship, this is as concentrated a dose of thriller mania as you will find. You’re gripping your chair just thinking about it, aren’t you?

George Miller had been mulling a new Mad Max film for years, and clearly, he spent that time coming up with every possible permutation of a chase sequence. This movie remains thrilling, almost insane, four years later.

Because of Ang Lee’s prestige and the glamorous international cast, there is sometimes a sense that this film is bland, good-for-you Important Filmmaking. But watch it again today. This movie is iconic for a reason: it's a blast, and a euphoric ride.

If the first installment was more of a gritty thriller, then T2 is where director James Cameron cranked up the action spectacle. (That’s the kind of thing that happens when you have a much bigger budget.) Harnessing the power of then-new CG technology, this sequel threw down a challenge at the start of the ‘90s that other blockbuster filmmakers struggled to answer.

Men in Black is that perfect mix of boot-chasing, gun-firing acton with so much outer-wordly originality, Hollywood is still trying to suck every last ounce of life-force out of the 1997 original. Can we just leave the classics alone?

Yes, the car chases are as amazing as you’ve heard, but what’s striking today is how well this holds up as a cop procedural. Steve McQueen was an incredible movie star, and he was never better than he was here.

Popeye Doyle is the perfect action star for the ‘70s: grizzled, cranky, morally compromised, not the least bit likable, but absolutely tenacious about getting the bad guy, even if it’s for reasons he can’t even necessarily comprehend. Gene Hackman was at the absolute peak of his powers at this point.

Hollywood remade Akira Kurosawa’s masterpiece as The Magnificent Seven. It couldn’t compare: Not only is Seven Samurai an epic of scope and scale, it’s one of the most emotionally nuanced of action movies, featuring a slew of characters you come to care deeply about.

Michael Mann’s epic is the culmination of everything he’d been working toward his entire career; the years since still feel like his own response to it. Everybody remembers the diner scene, but the bank heist sequence feels like a magic trick even more today.

#4886. Privacy coins face diverging fortunes as KuCoin moves to drop Monero

KuCoin has already suspended XMR deposits and plans to close withdrawals on Dec. 31. XMR fell 10.5% to $449.98 as of 7:00 p.m. UTC on Thursday. The drop extends a decline from about $625 on Nov. 3.

Launched in 2014, Monero conceals transaction amounts and the wallet addresses of senders and recipients by default. Unlike Monero, Zcash (ZEC), launched in 2016, allows users to choose between transparent and shielded transactions. Both cryptocurrencies have faced regulatory scrutiny over the past few years, with Binance delisting Monero in 2024 and Kraken ending support for it in the European Economic Area later that year.

Zach Pandl, head of research at Grayscale, which launched the first US spot ZEC exchange-traded fund (ETF) in August, said Zcash is positioned differently from Monero. He told Cointelegraph that the firm’s commitment to Zcash will continue for “many years to come.”

Related: Bitwise seeks Texas Stock Exchange listing for Zcash ETF

Pandl said that viewing keys allow Zcash holders to disclose transactions “to an auditor or regulator, law enforcement if they need.” He said the feature gives users greater control over who can access their financial information. “That is exactly how the financial system works today. It’s just that it gives the authority to individuals rather than institutions,” he said.

However, whether viewing keys alone can satisfy regulatory requirements remains a point of debate.

Pandl said that as AI has advanced, it has become “much easier to link pseudonymous addresses with offchain information.” Monero, he explained, uses ring signatures that obscure the source of transactions among multiple possible signers, a method Pandl said “may be vulnerable” as AI-powered blockchain analytics improve.

“We believe strongly that Zcash is the stronger tech,” he said, because “it takes a shielding approach rather than an obfuscation approach.” Zcash uses zero-knowledge proofs to verify shielded transactions without publicly revealing sensitive transaction data onchain.

Grayscale’s ETF reached $1 billion in assets under management on Sept. 24, but that figure had fallen to $406 million on Wednesday. Zcash more than tripled in value this year, rising to $1,653 on Sept. 26 from $524 on Jan. 1, according to Token Terminal data. Its price more than doubled in the month following the ETF’s launch but has since fallen back to $770. The cryptocurrency remains up about 50% year to date.

Pandl described Zcash’s price appreciation over the past year as “Bitcoin’s Solana moment,” referring to Solana’s growing market cap and its challenge to Ethereum’s dominance as the “leading smart contract platform.”

“At 1.2% of Bitcoin’s market cap, I would still consider Zcash at a relatively low value,” he said, adding that Grayscale has no price targets for ZEC.

#4885. Ethereum Sets December 15 Date for Delayed Glamsterdam Testnet Upgrade

Ethereum Sets December 15 Date for Delayed Glamsterdam Testnet Upgrade

Ethereum developers have scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi test network for December 15, 2026, more than a month after security concerns forced them to call off the fork.

The upgrade will activate on Hoodi at 19:12 UTC that day, at epoch 143,616, developers agreed during an All Core Devs Consensus (ACDC) call on Thursday, according to an AI-generated summary of the meeting and notes from tracker EIPsInsight. They chose December 15 over December 16.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short ETH with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Client teams on both the execution and consensus layers are expected to cut releases for the fork by early next week.

The upgrade has already gone live on Sepolia, another Ethereum test network, where it began producing blocks in October with a gas limit more than three times mainnet's. Developers have not yet set a date for mainnet.

The Hoodi fork was originally due on October 26, but developers postponed it after security firm ChainSecurity warned that Glamsterdam's gas changes could weaken safeguards in existingsmart contracts, citing 13 real-world examples.

At the center of the concerns is EIP-8037, which raises the cost of creating new data on Ethereum to slow the growth of the network's state, the data every node must store, as block gas limits rise. It also meters that cost separately from other computation, which allows gas to be returned to a contract during execution, something some existing contracts' security checks do not expect.

After reviewing feedback from execution layer clients, developers reached rough consensus on Thursday to ship EIP-8037 as is, rather than delay the upgrade further or change the specification, though some participants raised concerns about potential breakage and the usefulness of the GAS opcode, which reports how much gas remains in a transaction.

Under the proposal, creating a new account would cost about seven times as much gas as it does today, and deploying a 24 kB contract about eight times as much. Its authors said the change would cap state growth at a target of about 120 GiB a year at a 150 million gas limit.

Consensus layer teams also agreed on a fix for how they validate blocks from builders, picking a less disruptive option that most teams considered a stopgap over a cleaner solution that would have required a consensus-breaking change.

Developers did not decide whether to keep FOCIL, a proposal designed to make it harder for block builders to censor transactions, as a headline feature of Hegotá, Ethereum's next upgrade after Glamsterdam.

Some participants argued that FOCIL should be dropped to free up resources for work to protect Ethereum against future quantum computers, while others said both could be developed in parallel. FOCIL keeps its status as a headline feature until the next ACDC call, around December 10, when developers expect to decide Hegotá's full scope.

Developers agreed to give post-quantum and AI security threats higher priority, at what the summary described as a "DEFCON 2-3" level of urgency. The Ethereum Foundation has said AI posed a more urgent threat to the network than quantum computing.

Wandering through the ruins of Pompeii, the ancient Roman city frozen in time by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, one is struck by that civilization’s devotion to precious materials. A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

Kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying new stones,” Kolodziejczak says.

Kalshi Courts Small Businesses With 'Microinsurance' as State Crackdowns Bite

Prediction market Kalshi is pitching its platform to small businesses as a form of insurance, as legal fights with states over its sports contracts mount.

About 500 businesses have used Kalshi to hedge risks ranging from commodity price swings to extreme weather and power outages, Nicolas Hull, the company's director of business development, told the Financial Times. Hull described the offering as "almost a form of microinsurance," but said almost all of the small businesses he had spoken to had never hedged before.
