#4858. 4 Scary Bitcoin Charts That Suggest This Bear Market Is Different

4 Scary Bitcoin Charts That Suggest This Bear Market Is Different

Bitcoin fell below $60,000 again on Friday as roughly $6.8 billion worth of Bitcoin options expired on derivatives exchange Deribit earlier in the day.

The largest cryptocurrency by market cap was trading at around $59,576 as of writing, down 1.58% on the daily chart after reaching an intraday high of $62,210.

As you might be able to guess based on the recent price action, Bitcoin's technical setup remains bearish—and there’s four charts in particular that tell the story.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The coin is trading well below its 50-day and 200-day exponential moving averages, or EMAs, which currently sit at $71,112 and $74,444, respectively, with the shorter-term average below the longer-term one—a classically bearish death cross pattern.

Its Relative Strength Index, or RSI, which measures the strength of recent price movements on a scale of 0 to 100, sits at 25.69, putting Bitcoin in oversold territory. Bitcoin is also approaching its 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level at $57,618, a potential support derived from the cryptocurrency's rally between its 2022 bottom and 2025 peak.

A sustained break below that level would put the recent lows back in focus. The next major Fibonacci retracement on the chart sits near $39,000, which would be an absolute nightmare for the markets. Thankfully for Bitcoin holders, BTC has bounced every time it touched it.

Perhaps more concerning for long-term Bitcoin investors, however, is what's happening to some of the most popular models used to make sense of Bitcoin's historical price cycles.

The Bitcoin Power Law model, popularized by physicist Giovanni Santostasi, attempts to explain Bitcoin's price growth as a mathematical function of its age.

Plotting Bitcoin's price and the time elapsed since its creation on logarithmic scales produces a relatively straight trend line. Two parallel lines establish theoretical upper and lower boundaries based on historical price extremes.

The appeal of the model was that Bitcoin's increasingly expensive bear market bottoms appeared remarkably predictable, despite the cryptocurrency's notorious volatility.

Bitcoin is now trading below what crypto analytics provider Bitbo sets as the theoretical support line of approximately $68,600, while the model's central regression puts its price near $193,400.

That's roughly 69% below its theoretical valuation, and 13% below what was supposed to be its historical floor.

The breach challenges one of the model's most attractive assumptions: that Bitcoin's minimum price increases predictably over time.

Bitcoin's four-year market cycle revolves around the halving, a programmed event that cuts the issuance of new Bitcoin tokens by 50% approximately every four years.

The most recent halving, in April 2024, reduced the reward miners receive for producing a block from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC.

Bitbo's post-halving comparison chart takes the price performance following the 2012, 2016 and 2020 halvings and adjusts those returns to Bitcoin's price at the start of the 2024 cycle.

Had Bitcoin replicated its performance following the 2020 halving, it would currently be trading somewhere around $140,000. Matching the returns of its earlier cycles would imply prices of several hundred thousand dollars or more.

Instead, roughly 950 days after its most recent halving, Bitcoin is trading below where it was when that cycle began.

Diminishing returns are nothing new for Bitcoin as the asset grows larger. But the scale of the current underperformance raises questions about how useful previous halving cycles remain as a guide to future returns.

It also shows traders are a bit less enthusiastic about the upcoming halving vs previous times—maybe because Bitcoin is now more mainstream and the user base is more diverse and less interested in those technicalities.

The Bitcoin Rainbow Chart, which originated in 2014, uses logarithmic price curves and colored bands to classify Bitcoin's historical valuation.

The upper red bands represent speculative bubbles, while the lower blue and violet bands indicate historically depressed prices.

Bitcoin's price has dropped beneath even the violet region, humorously labeled “Bitcoin Dead,” in the supplied chart.

This isn't the first time the Rainbow Chart has struggled to accommodate Bitcoin's price movements. Its creator revised the model in November 2022 after the previous version failed to contain that year's market collapse.

The chart is ultimately a visualization of historical price behavior rather than a scientifically validated valuation model. Its latest divergence is another reminder of that limitation.

Bitbo's price prediction comparison brings together four different approaches to estimating Bitcoin's long-term value.

The Stock-to-Flow model, introduced by pseudonymous analyst PlanB in 2019, measures scarcity by comparing Bitcoin's existing supply with its annual issuance. Stock-to-Income expands on that concept by incorporating miners' transaction fee revenue and regularly updating its calculations.

The Power Law measures price growth over time, while the Halving Price Regression fits a curve using historical prices at halving dates, excluding much of the speculative activity between them.

In the chart's late-2026 projections, Stock-to-Flow puts Bitcoin near $397,535, followed by the Power Law at $198,495, Stock-to-Income at $173,412, and Halving Price Regression at $141,132.

Bitcoin is trading approximately 85% below the most optimistic of those projections and 58% below even the most conservative one.

None of these models directly measures how much money investors are willing to put into Bitcoin today, and arguably Bitcoin is now a different asset than the BTC we used to follow two years ago.

It’s possible that after the wave of ETFs, funds, derivatives, 401Ks, regulations, indicators tracking its price, and widespread access to retail investors, it’s these price-prediction models that need to change.

#4854. Could AI Break Bitcoin? Not Yet, Research Firm K33 Says

Could AI Break Bitcoin? Not Yet, Research Firm K33 Says

Recent AI-assisted advances in mathematics have reignited worries about the cryptography underpinning Bitcoin, but there’s no evidence the network’s security has actually been broken, according to a report from research and brokerage firm K33.

The analysts, writing Friday, said AI’s rapid progress in math warrants closer attention to Bitcoin’s defenses, while cautioning against mistaking theoretical breakthroughs for a practical attack.

“Naturally, this has reignited fears surrounding the mathematical assumptions underpinning Bitcoin and modern cryptography,” they wrote, adding that the developments do not themselves offer a way to crack those systems.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The spark was a draft proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of math’s most famous open problems, published last week by Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge with help from the company’s Claude model.

As Decrypt reported, the proof passed independent computational verification, though academic review is ongoing. Its arrival stoked speculation about whether AI could eventually unravel the math securing digital assets.

K33 pushed back on the alarm. Bitcoin’s transaction signatures rely on elliptic curve cryptography, which hinges on how hard it is to derive a private key from a public one, even though the reverse is easy.

The firm noted that the Riemann proof provides no method for attacking that, and that the deeper “P versus NP” question at the heart of such fears remains unsolved. Even if someone proved P equals NP, K33 said, that wouldn’t necessarily yield a usable algorithm, or one that could run fast enough to recover a private key in any practical timeframe.

Conversely, proving P does not equal NP wouldn’t guarantee Bitcoin’s safety either, since faster attack algorithms could still emerge.

The report lands as the broader industry takes the AI-cryptography threat increasingly seriously. The Ethereum Foundation recently flagged AI as a more urgent danger than quantum computing, given its ability to find software flaws and sharpen existing algorithms.

K33 noted the Ethereum Foundation has doubled its protocol security team and recommended the Keccak-256 hash function for a post-quantum transition it aims to complete by 2029.

The takeaway, per K33, is vigilance without panic.

AI’s mathematical leaps deserve monitoring, and crypto networks are right to harden their cryptography against future threats, but as things stand, Bitcoin’s defenses remain as sound as they were at launch, with no demonstrated compromise.

Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) supervised by the Austrian Financial Market Authority (FMA) reported 20.4 billion euros ($22.37 billion) in trading volume for the first half of 2026.

About 74% of user accounts on these platforms were based in other European Economic Area (EEA) countries, particularly Germany and France, the Austrian financial supervisor said in a press release on Friday.

OpenAI has turned the tables on Apple, filing a countersuit that accuses the iPhone maker of stealing its trade secrets and pressuring hardware suppliers to freeze the ChatGPT maker out, escalating a legal brawl over the race to build the next must-have AI gadget.

The counterclaims, filed Friday in federal court in San Jose, California, flip the script on a dispute Apple started in July, when it sued OpenAI, its io Products hardware unit and two former Apple employees, Tang Tan and Chang Liu, accusing them of carrying confidential hardware secrets to OpenAI to help build a competing device.

OpenAI denied those claims and cast Apple’s suit as an attempt to choke off its ability to hire Apple talent.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic, Nvidia, Microsoft and more with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Now OpenAI is alleging misconduct of Apple’s own. In the filing, the company accuses Apple of “coercing and threatening” suppliers that work with both firms, including asking shared manufacturers to identify which personnel were assigned to OpenAI projects and pressuring at least one vendor to stop work.

OpenAI also claims a former OpenAI employee who returned to Apple took details about its product plans and suppliers with them, an inversion of Apple’s original accusation.

The countersuit brings claims including federal trade-secret theft, interference with contracts and unfair competition under California law. OpenAI argues Apple sued because it is losing the AI race, asserting in the complaint that the company “has struggled to incorporate innovative AI capabilities into its previously popular products” and is trying to “compete unfairly by any means available.”

It also contends Apple’s employment and exit policies create “trapdoors” designed to let it accuse departing staff of theft.

The reciprocal accusations underscore how high the stakes have climbed in the contest to define the hardware of the AI era. The earlier phase of the case grew contentious over discovery, with OpenAI’s internal emails and text messages drawn into the fight.

A judge indicated the court was “highly likely” to grant Apple’s request for a preliminary injunction, and in October OpenAI pledged not to use the Apple trade secrets at the center of the suit.

Apple has previously said its investigation turned up no OpenAI confidential information. Its original lawsuit is set for trial on July 19, 2027.

#4850. Brazil’s stock exchange pushes stablecoin launch back to 2027

Brazil’s stock exchange is working with six major financial institutions on a real-backed stablecoin that could launch as early as the first quarter of 2027.

Brazil’s stock exchange B3 is moving ahead with 2027 plans for a stablecoin pegged to the Brazilian real, after initially targeting a launch this year.

B3 is collaborating with six of Brazil’s largest financial institutions, Bradesco, BTG Pactual, Itaú Unibanco, Safra, Santander and XP, to launch the stablecoin in the first quarter of 2027, according to a Friday report by local news outlet Valor Econômico.

Called Open BRL, the stablecoin is to be issued by Banco B3, the exchange’s banking subsidiary, with each token backed by one Brazilian real. B3 will operate the underlying technology.

The initiative marks a new stage in the exchange’s digital asset strategy as Brazil’s financial industry prepares to bring traditional securities onto blockchain networks.

B3 first disclosed plans to introduce its own stablecoin in December 2025, targeting a launch in 2026.

As recently as July, the exchange was reportedly still preparing to launch a stablecoin called B3RL in the coming months, with infrastructure testing and integration with financial institutions scheduled for August and September.

B3RL was designed to be backed by Brazilian reais and secured by government bonds, and to facilitate blockchain-based trading of stocks and fixed-income securities starting in 2027.

It remains unclear whether Open BRL will replace B3RL or operate alongside it. Cointelegraph reached out to B3 for clarification but had not received a response by publication.

B3 also plans to introduce trading of tokenized shares in early 2027, initially using the same order book as conventional equities.

The platform would initially retain its two-business-day settlement cycle rather than introduce instant settlement, Humberto Costa, a B3 executive overseeing digital asset products, reportedly said in October.

Related: Brazil’s Halloween eve crypto deadline brings more tricks than treats

Costa also said B3RL would not handle settlement of tokenized shares at launch and that round-the-clock trading would require changes to Brazil’s regulatory framework.

Brazil’s Securities and Exchange Commission has been exploring a new regulatory framework for tokenization, presenting the progress of its dedicated working group at an industry meeting in October.

#4845. Binance to launch tokenized IPO program after regulatory approval: Yi He

Binance is hiring for equity capital markets roles, including an analyst to develop tokenized equity products and assess prospective issuers.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance plans to launch a tokenized initial public offering (IPO) program for onchain share issuance once it receives regulatory approval.

The project forms part of Binance’s real-world asset strategy and will involve collaboration with decentralized finance projects, Binance co-founder and co-CEO Yi He said during BNB Demo Night in Bangkok on Friday.

“Actually, that’s a professional IPO process,” He said, distinguishing the planned program from simply listing new assets on the exchange.

Her comments follow Binance’s recent job postings for equity capital markets roles, which fueled speculation about the exchange’s plans to facilitate onchain IPOs.

One job posting seeks an equity capital markets research analyst to help develop tokenized equity products, evaluate prospective issuers and assess deal structures, pricing and allocation. The role requires at least four years of relevant experience and an understanding of traditional IPOs and follow-on offerings.

Cointelegraph reached out to Binance for further details but had not received a response by publication.

#4839. What was Coinbase worth while Nasdaq was closed?

A Thanksgiving buyer paid 106.24 USDC per Coinbase share. Whether that looked like a holiday rally depended on when you’d last checked the stock.

Tokenized stocks give investors another place to trade after the closing bell. Coinbase’s Thanksgiving tape shows why it still matters where else the shares changed hands and how many you want to trade.

On Thanksgiving afternoon, a buyer spent 125.49 USDC (USDC) on tokenized Coinbase shares while Nasdaq was closed. If you’d last checked the stock at Wednesday’s closing bell, that small purchase seemed to carry news of a holiday rally.

Coinbase had closed at $103.72, and the buyer on OKXICE paid 106.24 USDC per token, an apparent gain of 2.4%. But if you’d stayed for Wednesday’s after-hours session, you’d have seen the shares reach $106.91, according to brokerage Public.

From there, the very same token trade looked about 0.6% lower, valuing USDC at a dollar. However, the choice of where to start measuring was enough to turn a gain into a decline.

Related: Nasdaq exec pushes for common EU rules on tokenized securities

An investor in Germany had an even fresher price to go on. Early on Thanksgiving, 142 Coinbase shares changed hands on Tradegate at 97.50 euros apiece, roughly $107 at that day’s exchange rate.

What changed for the afternoon buyer was that they could open a wallet and buy Coinbase exposure over the holiday, and anyone following the stock could see exactly what that order cost.

Finding oneself on the other side of that trade with $10,000 worth of Coinbase to sell, the blockchain could tell you to four decimal places what someone had paid for just over one token, but could you get that price for 94?

#4832. China sets March 2027 rollout for blockchain identity regulations

China published new regulations on blockchain-based digital identities on Nov. 27, establishing a framework for identity verification and interoperability across government institutions and private-sector platforms.

The regulations, which will take effect on March 1, 2027, were jointly issued by 11 government departments, including the People’s Bank of China and the Cyberspace Administration of China.

Under the rules, China’s national blockchain network will provide the infrastructure for a digital identity system operated by entities authorized by the country’s cyberspace regulator, in cooperation with identity authentication and credential providers.

Digital identities powered by blockchain technology can allow users to verify their identity or credentials across platforms without disclosing unnecessary personal information.

According to Chinese state-backed media outlet China Net, the identity chain will bring together multiple institutions “to achieve multi-party consensus through blockchain technology.”

The regulations are part of China’s broader push to expand blockchain adoption, with the country targeting 2030 to largely complete its national blockchain infrastructure while maintaining restrictions on cryptocurrency-related activities in mainland China.

Individuals and organizations will be able to voluntarily register digital identities and use verifiable credentials to disclose specific information, such as educational or professional qualifications, without necessarily revealing all the associated data.

Platforms and digital identity service providers will be required to follow data minimization requirements, collecting only the information necessary for identity verification. They will be prohibited from using that data for cross-platform profiling or targeted advertising.

The regulations aim to address barriers to identity verification across regions, industries and platforms. They also encourage interoperability with digital yuan and the adoption of distributed digital identities in sectors including finance, taxation, transportation and customs.

Related: China targets 2030 for its national blockchain network buildout

#4830. The AD Team's Favorite Tea Kettle

I initially bought the Fellow Stagg EKG Electric Kettle amid my latest health kick: I'd read somewhere (see: watched an Instagram Reel) that oolong tea can help ease bloating and support digestion. (For what it’s worth, there’s also a bit of science behind the claim.) I already had a ton of Dona oolong tea at my office desk, so a desktop kettle seemed like a natural purchase for completing the setup. My plan was to have a cup of oolong at 4 p.m. every day. While my daily tea service lasted about 10 days before I forgot about it, the kettle has stayed a fixture of my routine, and, as it turns out, many members of my team's routine, too.

Coworkers ask to use my kettle often enough that I’ve stopped thinking of it as entirely mine. Using it means you don’t have to walk all the way to the Condé Nast kitchen station, there's almost never any line, and the adjustable temperature means you can brew French press coffee, green tea, black tea, or any herbal blend you're working through at the right heat. The kettle is especially popular around the 3 p.m. slump, when everyone needs a quick caffeine hit to finish out the day before hustling off to their evening events.

As kettles go, the Fellow Stagg is a good-looking one: Made up of a matte body, slim gooseneck spout, and small control screen, it doesn't call attention to itself on a desk. the kettle also comes in more than half a dozen colors, allowing it to blend into most spaces.

Senior commerce editor Nashia Baker, a self-proclaimed "a social tea and coffee drinker," uses her Fellow at home. She likes displaying her beverage supplies so guests can make their own cup when they come over, and she credits the spout and ergonomic handle with "a steady, even pour" that spreads hot water equally over coffee grounds or a tea sachet. That control is the whole point of a gooseneck, which is designed for pour-over coffee.

The feature I didn't expect to love was the hold setting, which keeps water hot for 15 to 60 minutes after it boils. In an office setting, this capability makes the difference between a warm cup of tea and a cold one you forgot about during a meeting that ran long. The 30-ounce capacity also means the second and third person in line for a fresh mug don't have to wait for a new boil.

I won't claim a kettle will change your life, but mine has at least endeared me to my coworkers. If you've been considering buying one, now is a good time, as it's 20% off for Black Friday. May we all enjoy our 4 p.m. oolongs all winter long.

#4829. Bitcoin whales pile into BTC despite shrinking profit cushion

CryptoQuant data shows Bitcoin whales are breaking with historical fourth-quarter selling patterns despite a market downturn.

Bitcoin whales are bucking the years-long trend of trimming their balances toward the end of the year. Instead, they are accumulating the cryptocurrency despite falling prices and dwindling unrealized profits.

According to onchain analytics firm CryptoQuant, whales added about 121,000 Bitcoin (BTC) to their holdings between Sept. 30 and Nov. 21, taking their combined balance to nearly 2.95 million BTC, despite a price decline of nearly 30% over the same period.

CryptoQuant defines whales as addresses holding between 1,000 and 10,000 BTC. Unrealized profits across addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC have shrunk 81% to $23.8 billion from $124.7 billion on Sept. 30.

The report, supported by crypto lending platform CoinRabbit, notes that whales have historically reduced their holdings toward the end of the year in both bull and bear markets. Since 2017, whale balances have declined in seven of the nine previous fourth quarters, with 2019 and 2020 being the only exceptions.

Meanwhile, dolphins, a term referring to addresses holding between 100 and 1,000 BTC, have slightly reduced their holdings. The group shed about 15,169 BTC, representing 0.28% of its holdings.

Related: Bitcoin supply metric hits 11-year low as new ‘capitulation’ signal arrives

The accumulation comes as Bitcoin has lost about 32% of its value since the beginning of the year, with the cryptocurrency trading at around $59,750 at 6:45 p.m. UTC on Friday, according to TradingView data. The report notes that borrowing against Bitcoin holdings may be allowing some large investors to access liquidity without selling their assets.

According to CryptoQuant, among CoinRabbit users with more than $100,000 in loans, the number of Bitcoin-backed loans increased by 298.9% month-on-month in October, while total loan volume fell by 16.2%.

The pattern contrasts with October 2025, when the number of Bitcoin-backed loans fell by 3.7% but total loan volume increased by 122.8%.

CryptoQuant suggested that the shift toward more frequent but smaller loans could indicate that large holders are borrowing to raise cash instead of selling Bitcoin.

Crypto tax firm Summ suggested the shift could also be linked to the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). Since January, participating jurisdictions have begun requiring crypto exchanges and other service providers to collect users’ transaction data for tax authorities, with the first international exchanges of tax-related information expected in 2027.

Summ CEO Shane Brunette said holding BTC and borrowing against it are rational responses “to a world where every sale is visible.”

#4826. Franklin Templeton makes room for HYPE in crypto index ETF

The addition comes as US spot investment products tracking Hyperliquid’s native token reach $266.5 million in assets under management.

Asset manager Franklin Templeton plans to add the Hyperliquid (HYPE) token to its crypto index exchange-traded fund (ETF), according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Nov. 25.

The token will be added to the Franklin Crypto Index ETF on Dec. 1, following HYPE’s inclusion in the fund’s benchmark. The fund, which trades under the ticker EZPZ, currently holds Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), XRP, Solana (SOL), Dogecoin (DOGE), Cardano (ADA) and Lumen (XLM).

Hyperliquid, a layer-1 blockchain that hosts a decentralized exchange specializing in perpetual futures trading, has seen its total value locked rise to $7.3 billion from $4.13 billion in early January. The protocol generated $80.3 million in revenue over the past 30 days, according to DefiLlama.

Its native token, HYPE, is used to pay network fees and can be staked to earn rewards. The protocol also uses a portion of its trading fee revenue to buy back HYPE on the open market, linking trading activity on the platform to demand for the token.

Related: HYPE teases all-time high as NYSE owner ICE eyes US Hyperliquid perps

Franklin Templeton’s move comes as more investment products offer exposure to HYPE.

Three US spot exchange-traded products (ETPs) tracking HYPE have launched since May, with offerings from asset managers 21Shares, Bitwise and Grayscale. They collectively held approximately $266.5 million in assets under management as of Nov. 27, according to Coinperps data.

These products allow US investors to gain exposure to the Hyperliquid ecosystem through traditional financial rails without having to directly hold the token.

The exchange ranks among the largest venues for decentralized perpetual futures trading, although its official interface remains restricted to US users. Perpetual futures are derivative contracts that allow traders to speculate on an asset’s price movements without a fixed expiration date.

President Donald Trump said in August that Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig was working to bring Hyperliquid into the US in compliance with regulations.

#4825. Here’s what happened in crypto today

Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

Today in crypto, Bitcoin whales have added about 121,000 BTC since the end of September, defying historical year-end selling patterns. Meanwhile, the EU’s securities watchdog plans to make it easier to verify which crypto companies are authorized to operate in the bloc, and crypto bug bounty platforms are expanding their use of AI to identify genuine security threats amid a surge in submissions.

Bitcoin whales are bucking the years-long trend of trimming their balances toward the end of the year. Instead, they are accumulating the cryptocurrency despite falling prices and dwindling unrealized profits.

According to onchain analytics firm CryptoQuant, whales added about 121,000 Bitcoin (BTC) to their holdings between Sept. 30 and Nov. 21, taking their combined balance to nearly 2.95 million BTC, despite a price decline of nearly 30% over the same period.

CryptoQuant defines whales as addresses holding between 1,000 and 10,000 BTC. Unrealized profits across addresses holding at least 1,000 BTC have shrunk 81% to $23.8 billion from $124.7 billion on Sept. 30.

The report, supported by crypto lending platform CoinRabbit, notes that whales have historically reduced their holdings toward the end of the year in both bull and bear markets. Since 2017, whale balances have declined in seven of the nine previous fourth quarters, with 2019 and 2020 being the only exceptions.

Meanwhile, dolphins, a term referring to addresses holding between 100 and 1,000 BTC, have slightly reduced their holdings. The group shed about 15,169 BTC, representing 0.28% of its holdings.

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) is preparing an overhaul of its public crypto register nearly two years after its launch.

The European Union’s securities watchdog plans to replace its manual interim register under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) with a searchable web-based platform around mid-2027, an ESMA spokesperson told Cointelegraph.

The new system will also maintain a version history for individual white papers to provide archives of changes.

MiCA’s transitional period ended in July, which meant that unauthorized crypto service providers had to wind down their EU operations or face multimillion-euro fines or other enforcement action. ESMA’s interim register serves as a public reference point for checking whether a crypto company is authorized in the bloc.

Crypto bug bounty platforms have expanded their use of artificial intelligence to keep up with a growing mountain of AI-assisted security reports.

Crypto-focused HackenProof said in October that it was using AI to triage 70% of submissions fully autonomously, aiming to hit 85% by the end of 2026. It said it received an average of about 6,100 bug reports a month in the third quarter, 2.4 times the reports from December last year.

Rival Immunefi last week said submissions to its platform rose 136% year-over-year in the first nine months of 2026, as it introduced a tool that can flag duplicates before a researcher submits a report.

Bug bounty programs pay independent researchers to find and report potential security flaws. AI has helped researchers uncover more genuine vulnerabilities, but has also swelled the volume of invalid and duplicate submissions, making it harder for security teams to identify the threats that need urgent attention.

It’s like “bringing a sword to a gunfight,” Dmitry Tokarev, founder of crypto wallet provider Bron, told Cointelegraph, referring to security teams that haven’t already adopted AI to sift through reports.

#4819. 5 Things We’re Saying No to This Holiday Season

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Before you say yes this holiday season, ask yourself what you’re saying yes to. Consider the feelings that come up for you when you think about it. Is it excitement about seeing the people you love? Is it dread at the anticipation of planning, conflict, or grief? For some, it’s all of the above.

Recent polls find that nearly 9 in 10 (89%) U.S. adults report holiday stressors (APA, 2023). Tensions arise due to finances, family conflict, grief, and other factors. Stress takes away from the pleasurable aspects of the season, which should include reconnection and rest.

Sometimes that is easier said than done. Here are 5 things we're saying no to this holiday season and strategies to achieve the happy holidays we deserve.

Sometimes that family holiday announcement sounds like a demand rather than an invitation. “Dinner is at 4 pm sharp. See you there!” Everyone assumes you’ll be there, and no one asks questions. They don’t ask if you can take time off work, afford the trip, or have other plans. You feel obligated to attend despite any barriers you are facing.

Almost no one will tell you that you are allowed to consider your own needs before you RSVP yes. Ask yourself whether you have the time, energy, and money to participate this year. If the answer is no, it’s alright. Your family may be disappointed, and you may feel a little guilty, but it’s worth asking which will weigh on you more: the guilt of saying no or the cost of saying yes.

In toxic families, it’s the once-over as soon as you enter the room. Before you’ve even had a chance to sit down, someone has made a joke about your weight or graying hair, offered a backhanded compliment about the dish you contributed, or slipped in a dig about your personal life.

You may feel hurt, sad, or even angry, and you don’t have to ignore those feelings to preserve the holiday spirit. You can be silent and stone-faced to let the “joke” fall flat. You might excuse yourself and regroup in another room. If you want to address it directly and call out the hidden meaning, you can say, “That felt like a dig,” or ask, “What do you mean by that?” What you don’t have to do is tolerate disrespect.

When you want everyone to feel loved, it’s easy to slip into spending more than you intended. If you’ve ever hosted a large family gathering, you know how quickly the groceries and gifts add up. And if you’re the one who hosts every year, it can feel like the work and the bill are yours by default.

Before you do anything, set a budget. Then share the work in ways that play into everyone’s strengths. Maybe enlist the nephew who can roast meat or the cousin who loves to bake, and assign cleanup to the one you prefer to stay out of the kitchen. Suggest rotating hosting duties. Do a gift exchange rather than buying individual gifts for everyone. You can show your love to your family with limits.

In some families, playing the dutiful daughter (or son) means everyone assumes you’ll make the holidays happen. Often it’s the family matriarch or the eldest daughter who initiates the first call about the holiday plans and is the one still in the kitchen long after everyone else has gone home. She is the family “glue” who keeps track of the invites, remembers who can’t eat what, and figures out where to seat the relatives who aren’t speaking. By the time the holiday arrives, she’s too tired to enjoy the fruits of her labor.

If that sounds like you, name it. People who have never hosted may not realize all of the hidden effort that goes into an event. Bring it to their attention. Set limits on what you will do and ask for help, but don’t micromanage. If the person assigned to bring the rolls forgets, skip the rolls this year. If no one steps up, step back anyway. Plan a smaller, more intimate gathering that won’t leave you frazzled at the end of it.

The holidays aren’t the same after you’ve lost a loved one, and the first holiday season after a loss can be especially difficult. Family traditions may be upended. The person who always hosted and made everyone’s favorite dish is gone. Tensions that surface after the loss may still be hanging in the air.

Take a moment to evaluate your feelings. Ask yourself what you feel up to this year. Maybe it’s not the year to take on hosting duties, or perhaps you stop by for dessert rather than staying the entire day. You can choose to honor your loved one by retaining old traditions or step into the next chapter with new traditions in their memory. You can miss someone deeply and still make room for moments of joy this holiday season.

It might seem strange that saying no could be the start of a happy holiday. The beauty is that you get to decide what a happy holiday looks like for you, and that it can change from year to year. Ask yourself what would make the holidays feel good to you this year and do it.

American Psychological Association. (2023). Even a joyous holiday season can cause stress for most Americans. https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2023/11/holiday-season-stress

If Albany Park’s Kova sofa ranks high on your furniture wish list, now’s the time to clear some living room space. Recently reimagined by the brand, two distinct silhouettes make up the new Kova line: The Kova Box is the more structured of the two, with squared-off cushions that give the sofa a neatly defined profile, whereas the Kova Pillow offers softer contours and a more casual look. There’s 32 upholstery options available across each version, as well as the ability to dictate just how much you’ll sink into your sofa.

To sweeten the deal, the collection is included in Albany Park’s Black Friday sale, which runs through 12/6 and offers up to 30%, complimentary white-glove delivery, and three free throw pillows with any sofa purchase.

“I think of them as the same architecture with two different personalities,” says Paul DeVries, CEO of Albany Park. “Nobody buys a mattress without thinking about how firm or soft it is, [but] people have been buying sofas, particularly online, from photographs and a paragraph of copy. [And yet,] somehow, [they’re] expected to know exactly how that sofa is going to feel.”

The Kova’s modular design allows for a wide range of configurations, starting from a compact two-piece sofa, up to a six-piece U-shaped sectional. The redesign also includes a sturdier hardwood foundation and a more personalized approach to comfort. Equally noteworthy is the turnaround time. “Your Kova doesn’t exist until you order it,” says DeVries. As for how DeVries would configure his own Kova? He’s partial to the five-seat Box sectional with a left chaise and a storage ottoman (all the better for concealing spare blankets and pillows). Even with a dog who has a penchant for tracking the outdoors inside, he’s not inclined to forgo light-colored upholstery, believing that we shouldn’t be afraid to live with our furniture. “A sofa is one of the most important pieces of furniture in a home,” DeVries told us. “Something that important should feel more personal.”

BACK IN MY college days at Howard University, sweatpants were basically my uniform. I wore them to class, the dining hall, the computer lab, and pretty much anywhere I could get away with it. Look for soft, breathable materials like cotton, fleece, or jersey that keep you cozy but still allow for movement. Some performance fabrics wick moisture away and provide added durability.

Your best bet will be to find options with a waistband that won’t dig in and enough room in the thighs. Different styles offer different looks and levels of comfort, and understanding the options can help you select the right pair for your needs. Here’s a breakdown of the most common sweatpant fits.

The relaxed fit is all about breathability and unlimited mobility. These sweatpants offer extra room around the hips and thighs, providing a looser feel throughout the seat. It's ideal for lounging, casual wear, and people who prioritize comfort over a tailored look. Think of it as the ultimate chill-out pant—easygoing and roomy, perfect for a lazy day, lying around the house.

Tapered sweatpants are looser at the top (around the hips and thighs) but gradually get narrower toward the ankle. This creates a more streamlined, modern silhouette for active people who want to move easily while maintaining a fashionable appearance. These pants give off a sportier vibe, perfect for gym sessions, running errands, or looking good while staying comfortable.

Slim fit sweatpants are more form-fitting and cut closer to the body, especially in the thighs and calves. They offer a sleek, minimalist look without being as tight as leggings. They’re ideal for everyday wear and even casual work settings when paired with an appropriate top.

Joggers are a type of tapered sweatpant that features a cuff at the ankle. They often have a more athletic, streetwear-inspired look and are typically made from a thinner material. The hybrid look is favored among athleisure lovers and those who like a sporty, on-the-go aesthetic. Joggers are suitable for running, light workouts, or even running errands.

Features like hidden zippered pockets enhance functionality, especially for travel. Deep side pockets can be super handy for carrying your phone, keys, wallet, earbuds, or small bills while on the go. And if you’re being a couch potato for the weekend, you can stash your remote control or snack in there as well.

Our style team, led by Style Director Christian Gollayan, put each pair through real-life scenarios: casual hangouts, city commutes, travel days, and of course, workout sessions. To keep things fair, we created a rubric and scored them across four key categories: comfort, durability, fit, and versatility.

We assessed how soft and breathable they felt, how well they survived workouts and laundry days, whether they struck the right balance between relaxed and polished, and how easily they transitioned from our homes to the streets. Bonus points went to pairs with performance perks like stretch, moisture-wicking, quick-drying, and anti-odor protection. After all was said and done, we narrowed it down to eight selections that truly stood out.

Sweatpants tend to have a looser fit throughout the leg, while joggers feature a more tailored or tapered fit. This means the legs of joggers will often touch your skin and feel a bit tight if you’ve got beefy calves.

Traditional sweatpants are often made from thicker materials like fleece and have a casual appearance, while joggers can be made from a wider range of materials, including activewear fabrics like nylon or polyester.

Joggers have ribbed cuffs at the ankles and a sportier appearance compared to the relaxed vibe of traditional sweatpants, whereas sweatpants can have either an open design or ribbed cuffs.

Sweatpants have a more relaxed and traditional look, while joggers are designed with a sporty aesthetic, often featuring modern details like zipper pockets and paneling. And because of the difference in ankle cuffs and fit, sweatpants look more casual, whereas joggers look more elevated and sleek.

Joggers are versatile for both athletic and casual wear, while sweatpants are primarily associated with casual lounging and relaxation.

Sweatpants are typically ideal for cozy indoor activities, while joggers can transition from the gym to casual outings due to their sleeker appearance.

#4813. 8 Best Modular Sofas, Tested And Reviewed by AD's Editors 2026

At one time, a modular sofa looked like it could have been toy furniture—each section clearly delineated. Now, seamless design allows this category of sectionals to look like traditional couches that happen to come apart in easy-to-move pieces. Better yet, this style allows you to customize furniture as your space changes. Whether you’re moving from a small apartment into a spacious four-bedroom and need to grow your seating, or you want to downsize a hulking U-shaped basement sectional into a love seat for a bedroom nook, a modular sectional is the way to go.

Style options abound for sectionals, from the artsy armless Sarah Sherman Samuel design for Lulu and Georgia to the minimalist Castlery and the iconic “Chiclet” silhouette made with injection-molded cushions from Herman Miller.

Moving around the sofa pieces is a cinch with user-friendly connector mechanisms, like slide-in glides and easy-to-configure brackets. It took contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert less than 30 minutes to maneuver the pieces of both her Burrow and Cozey modular sectionals into place. Better yet, most of the best modular sofas on this list come with white-glove delivery, so all you have to do is open the door when it arrives.

You can go as big or as small as you’d like with the Jonathan Chaise Sectional from Castlery, a modular option that starts as a two-seater and builds out to accommodate up to six. “This sofa is incredibly comfortable and feels very well-made,” contributor Rachel Fletcher says in her review. “I’d actually say it’s closer to my mattress in terms of firmness—medium firm to firm—which I very much appreciate. It’s not the kind of sofa you’re going to sink into, quicksand-style, and there’s absolutely no sagging effect.

The minimal, low-slung sofa works great in an understated space and could also appeal to a household with kids and pets. “Castlery does offer swatches and fabric samples, but I went all in without testing first and wasn’t sure what a polyester blend might feel like,” she adds. “Thankfully, it’s very soft. It’s made to resemble wool, but without the itchiness or stiffness. The heathered fabric makes it look expensive and should also help hide stains.”

The Cozey Neptune is a modular sofa that’s a jack of all trades: It can be assembled in less than half an hour, pulls out into a sleeper in two minutes flat, has hidden storage under the cushions, and is available in performance fabrics that protect against spills. Alpert chose the sofa for all those reasons, but what ultimately made the Neptune such a keeper for her was its portability. “I had no problem bringing it into the basement,” she says in her review, despite some tight angles on the landing. “Anyone who lives in a walk-up, has a tight stairway, or has narrow doorways typical of older homes will love this piece.”

Once fully assembled, it proved to be as durable as it is good-looking, treading the line between minimalism and groundedness. “I am very skeptical of couches with cushions on the back because I know that these can collapse, and that will drive me crazy,” Alpert explains. “This back is tightly upholstered, but it comes with three lumbar cushions that have a nice spring to them.” After over a year of nearly daily use from two school-age kids (and their friends), her Neptune still looks pristine.

To make the best use of the Neptune’s full-size sleeper-sofa configuration, Alpert recommends springing for the brand’s Sleep Kit ($270), which includes a topper, fitted sheet, flat sheet, two pillows and pillowcases, and a comforter. All of this fits in the three storage compartments within the seat cushions, a “saving grace” in a house with linens galore, says Alpert.

This rounded-edge, injected-foam modular sofa—affectionally nicknamed “Chiclet”—epitomizes simplicity. It’s the ideal couch if you can’t stand saggy cushions or a wrinkly back. The re-launch of the original 1976 style from Herman Miller sofa designer Ray Wilkes preserves the postmodern splendor of the first edition, but offers new fabrics and colorways, including sunny recycled wool twill and textural viscose-wool bouclé in earthy palettes. Consider this iconic sofa more of an art form than just a place to sit, even if you can build out the two-seat into a spacious six-seat perch.

No need to agonize over whether you’re a left-chaise or a right-chaise person. This reversible design lets you change your mind. Slipcovered cushions provide a relaxed, lived-in look, while its compact footprint—set on a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) to be responsibly sourced—makes it an especially smart pick for apartments, condos, and cozy living rooms. The modules allow you to adjust from a three-piece sectional to a sprawling, six-piece L-shape that can host a party.

Go ahead and dramatically drop down on the Lena sofa; the armless design will keep you from awkwardly hitting the arms. This showstopper from Sarah Sherman Samuel, with artful beam legs and a foam-seat construction, allows for just enough bounce. And because the streamlined silhouette has no sharp corners, you can sit two pieces next to each other for a glorious extended bench seating suited for a large living room.

As seen in Broadway actress Barrett Wilbert Weed’s Brooklyn Heights home, Arhaus is known for statement furnishings, and the Coburn fits the bill for plush lounging in style. Its 22-inch seat depth and down-and-feather–blend cushion fill combine to create a nest that is the ultimate definition of cozy. It’s also a top pick for a family with pets or kids because it comes upholstered in Crypton, an ultra durable fabric that can withstand spills, stains, and snags.

With seven distinct seat pieces, more than 140 upholstery options, and four leg covers, this Serena & Lily sectional wins the customization game. Incorporating the new addition to the Norfolk family, a curved corner piece with a 28-inch seat, creates a sectional with a sleek silhouette worthy of a lounge, especially when you accent the setup with a well-endowed arm chair. Layer on a few throw pillows to create an illusion of a cozy pit for hibernating over the weekend.

The modular design of the Article Beta sectional can work for 13 different configurations, including a love seat chaise and an L-shaped sofa with a chaise. Your living room is truly a canvas to experiment with this sectional, upholstered in a durable blend of polyester, viscose, linen, and cotton that makes it perfect for hosting. While the Beta only comes in three colors—white, cypress green, and gray—you can easily dress it up with a woven throw or a cuddle blanket.

Which Brands Offer the Most Versatile Configurations for Modular Sofas?

Serena & Lily and and Castlery stand out in this respect for offering design-forward options in performance fabrics. Article notably offers many configurations and deep seats.

Are Luxury Modulars Pet- and Kid-Friendly?

Depending on the fabric in question, plenty of modular sectionals are pet- and kid-friendly. Performance fabrics are as kid- and pet-friendly as it gets, designed to be durable, stain-resistant, and easy to clean. Luxury leather sectionals can be less pet- or kid-friendly than those upholstered in performance fabrics, as leather is no match for pet nails, for example. Arhaus notably offers modular sectional styles upholstered in Crypton, which allows liquids to roll off, not penetrate into the seat. The material is also designed to prevent scents from seeping in, making it a go-to for a pet family.

#4811. 3 Things to Do When Your Adult Child Pulls Away

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Just last week, my parent coaching client looked at me quizzically while describing a recent text from her son. The text was just a photo of her son's dog wearing (or at least trying to wear) a cap of a major league baseball team. She said, "Dr. Jeff, it's been two months since I last heard from him, and of course, I immediately smiled when I saw the pic."

This hurt, Mom soon added, "But I had no idea what to do next." This client elaborated that her fingers led her to compose and immediately delete five responses prior to sending them. She added, "No matter what I do, he will pull away again, anyway."

The client above was struggling with how to respond after a long lag in communication with her adult child. She didn't know whether to joke about the cute picture, or tell her son she missed him, or ask further about Thanksgiving. For any parents in similar situations, it can be maddening to feel unsure about how to respond.

And, if you have not spoken to your adult child for over six months or even years, the absence of that relationship has a huge, seemingly constant presence. By this I mean that often in these partial or full-on estrangement situations, the reality is that minimal or no contact does not take away from the internal emotional upheaval that comes from the desire to reconnect.

It is easy to feel helpless in the face of not seeing your adult child or not having the level of connection that you value. In my parent coaching work, I encourage parents to focus on three things they can do no matter how long it's been since they last heard their grown child's voice.

Finish this sentence: "What I miss most about my grown child today is__________." Some parents might reply that they wish they knew how their son was doing. Maybe, as in the early example of the dog photo, a parent misses lighter moments of laughter. Maybe a song reminds you of your adult child.

Identifying what you miss is tangible and healthy because it helps you process difficult feelings like sadness, disappointment, nostalgia, or loneliness. For example, that treasured memory of you and your daughter going for a ride and belting out a shared favorite song may weigh heavily on your mind. Consider sharing these thoughts with trusted relatives, friends, a therapist, or a parent coach. Sometimes it helps to have someone just say, "Tell me more."

Some parents have been deeply hurt by how their adult child has treated them, and yes, sometimes the reasons for the distance are unclear, and this can feel maddening. At the same time, if you genuinely regret anything you said or did, you can be specific about what you're apologizing for while still honoring your own experience of what happened.

Consider your adult daughter saying to you, "When I tell you what bothered me that you did when I was growing up, you kept twisting it to make it my fault and giving me advice." You may remember trying to help. But hold on, because, at the same time, maybe you can recall trying to give her advice when she said, "Dad, can I finish my point?"

Looking at your own behaviors in this way gives you an honest point of reflection to start. You could then say, "I've been reflecting on times I rushed in to give you advice, and it got in the way of better understanding what you were going through, and I'm sorry." This type of dialogue not only shows that you are taking responsibility, but you are also modeling self-awareness to your adult child.

In my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!, I explore how easily a parent's regret can turn into a feeling of indebtedness. In the parent coaching trenches, I have seen how tempting it is for parents to promise their adult children something to bring them closer. Please keep in mind that you can offer a sincere apology and still take your time to decide what you can reasonably do or give. For parents who are totally out of contact, I suggest you write down what you regret and keep it private.

This third point is really hard for parents missing their adult children. If several messages go unanswered, give your adult child room to reach out. If they asked for no contact, honor that request. Believe it or not, adult children in these situations often share with me that they still love and even miss their parents, even when they outwardly state they want no contact. Just remember what I wrote above: The absence of contact still has a great presence in both your mind and that of your adult child.
