#4807. tk Best Ergonomic Office Chairs for a Stylish Workspace (2026)

There’s a reason I am most productive when working from an office, and it’s not the harsh lighting or lack of distractions: It’s my office chair. Previously, I was convinced that “ergonomic” was an empty buzzword used by chiropractors and human resources, but after working from a slew of supportive seats these last few years, I’m a believer. Ideally, office chairs combine a sophisticated aesthetic with a genuinely functional build—and both things can be true in the same design. Maybe that budget mesh chair you picked up from an office supply store does the job, but is it the right culture fit for the very curated aesthetic of your home? Fortunately, I’ve sourced the products that check all the boxes, because you deserve to feel just as productive in your guest room-slash-office space.

Over the years that the Shop AD team has been testing office chairs, often corralling the entire office to take a seat, we’ve expanded our search to curate a high-low selection that includes wallet-friendly picks, but also household names in the ergonomic space, like Herman Miller and Knoll. Our favorite options cosigned by design lovers—we are Architectural Digest after all—and those looking to cure that stubborn tech neck twinge, finally.

Our editors and writers have personally sat on, worked, and Zoomed from each of these picks, at the office and from their home desks. We can attest that not only are they attractive, but they will also provide structural support for your entire body, even through the longest meeting days and tightest deadlines.

As a general practice, the armrests on ergonomic office chairs tend to be bulky. Not so with the Branch Verve Chair, which stands out with its curvy S-shaped supports that give it some space-y, extraterrestrial appeal. The Verve is a newer and sportier model from the brand that set out to modernize dated office furniture (from standing desks to seating), and boasts a sleek breathable mesh back and some slender legs with casters for wheeling around the office.

Contributor Terri Williams notes that sitting for long periods of time is easy thanks to the V-shaped chair design that provides extra lumbar support. At just a hair shy of $600, this chair is also one of the most affordable picks on the list (so it’s a good fit for most people), and one of the most streamlined if you hate the look of typical corporate chairs. The svelte design is why we chose it as our top pick over the AD editor-beloved Ergonomic Chair Pro below, which might not be as visually appealing to the average person. “I can also adjust the height of the softly-padded armrests, the seat depth, the tilt, the tilt tension, and the padded lumbar support,” Williams says of the extra features here that put it into holy grail territory.

There’s a reason the Aeron is Herman Miller’s most beloved and recognizable office chair. The iconic design is truly supportive and customizable to fit your ideal comfort zones, with adjustable offerings from the armrests to the seat itself. The seat is almost bouncy, springing you upright and into the most ergonomic position possible. In her other office chair, shopping editor Audrey Lee sits on a cushion, but states that the Aeron balances support with real comfort. Contributor Zoë Sessums selected hers after a virtual fitting with an ergonomic expert at Herman Miller, who walked her through all the features. (Herman Miller offers an informative online gallery of both imagery and detailed videos if you’re unable to try out a chair in person.) Once the chair was delivered—no assembly required, it literally rolls out of the box—Sessums came away impressed with the power of the patented PostureFit SL back support, which encourages opening up the chest and shoulders, and tilts the pelvis slightly forward. “This chair will save your body,” she says. “It’s easy to see why people invest in supreme desk setups. I would recommend the Aeron chair again and again.”

A bad case of tech neck hates to see the Branch Ergo Pro coming. That’s because the chair’s fully customizable support system is calibrated to ensure that your posture is optimized, even during long hours in one fixed position. It offers 14 points of adjustments total (count ’em!) to keep you comfortable, from the seat height to the headrest for those who are blessed with longer limbs. And compared to the original version reviewed above, this one is far cushier on the seat and armrests, with seven additional points of adjustability. It is slightly less svelte and also slightly more expensive than its predecessor, the original Branch Ergonomic, which our tester Williams also loved for its ergonomic design.

Each of our editors took a spin on the Branch Ergo Pro (read our full review) and came away smitten with the adjustability points and glutes support of this “double-stuffed” chair. “I was especially fond of the arm rests that helped me achieve perfect elbow support with my laptop stand and that the adjustable tilt option gave me the freedom to stretch my back out whenever needed,” commerce editor Audrey Lee noted.

The only drawback is that the Ergo Pro needs assembly out of the box, and the construction process is a bit of a learning curve. Still, everything came together quickly in about 30 minutes or less and was easy enough to complete solo. Since it can be fully disassembled, it’s also a great option for frequent movers.

There’s a lot to like about Haworth’s Breck chair. Lee reported that it arrived swiftly in a large box that was simple to carry inside. The assembly won’t leave you frustrated either. You’ll find instructions on the flaps of the delivery box and Haworth has the same manual available on their website as well as a short video with step-by-step directions. The whole process literally takes less than a couple of minutes before you’re ready to put the chair in action.

Don’t be fooled by the easy assembly process, though, as this office chair is more advanced than meets the eye. “I first received the Breck during a heat wave and appreciated the ultra-breathable backrest which allowed a comfortable amount of air to flow through,” says Lee. But it’s all the adjustable features that stand out to her. Need more tilt? No problem. Wish the armrests were just a tad longer? Easy. Height? Seat depth? Lumbar support? Done, done, and done. And while these are all perks you would expect from a high-priced chair that costs over $1,000, the Breck supplies them at under $500.

A high price tag comes with great expectations—which the Asari chair met completely. Lee appreciated its attention to detail, which included the soft leather, the perfect amount of foam fill in the seat, and a backrest that makes it a treat to sit down and work. “The chair has noticeably softened in a delightful way that’s ultra-accommodating to my dimensions without feeling too sunken in or too stiff,” she says. Unlike leather executive office chairs that can read harsh or overly corporate, the Asari’s look is unparalleled. Lee “absolutely recommends” this chair to anyone looking to splurge on their home office. From physical appearance to practical use, it scores 10s across the board.

It’s rare for a truly ergonomic chair to look as good as the Herman Miller Management Chair does. I chose the brown checkerboard upholstery and stainless steel frame and, not to brag, but my coworkers have since declared FOMO, requesting fun office chairs of their own. Like most Herman Miller options, this chair is very adjustable—the features I focused on customizing to my liking were the seat height and the amount of recline the back can have (which is a lot, actually, I feel like I’m lying down if I push too hard). The back cushion has a bit more firmness to it than the ultra-plush seat cushion, which is great for posture correction and staying focused. While it’s a bit too soft for my all-day liking, I do appreciate the additional padding on days when I know I’ll be mostly stationary. I rarely need to adjust my position, and my knees never fall asleep, something that used to happen quite often in my too-tall office chair. Overall, the management chair is excellent for both a home and office environment. With over a dozen upholstery options, you won’t have to worry about the seat clashing with your existing decor—I find it a stylish midcentury alternative to the often all-black silhouettes that plague traditional offices.

For anyone in need of a custom office chair, Steelcase has solutions. Senior commerce editor Nashia Baker settled on this grey leather version from 23 upholstery options, which allow you to choose from peachy pinks, neutrals, and warm leather hues. The overall silhouette is narrower than most, but the armrests are adjustable and the seat has a soft, gentle glide when maneuvered up or down. Even the wheels are smooth when rolling over floors, carpet or tile. “This chair has literally made the trek with me across the Condé Nast office and on various floors, though I haven’t noticed the wheels wearing or jamming in the months I’ve been testing it,” Baker says. With its stable, upright backrest, the seat discourages slouching, but also has enough give for comfortably sitting hour after hour. At over $2,000, it’s definitely an investment, but for all the custom flourishes, Baker says it’s all worth it.

For those in search of a no frills office chair, this West Elm one is sleek and simple. This is the least adaptable option on this list, in that it doesn’t allow for any other heights or tilts. What it lacks in ergonomic adjustment points, however, it makes up for in design prowess. The sleek stainless steel frame and leather seat make a more eye-catching pair, while the true-ball wheels roll smoothly and without catching on the carpet in the AD office. This is definitely for those who prefer a firmer seat and I liked how upright this office chair felt, like it was almost correcting my posture while encouraging a better sense of productivity. My colleague, shopping editor Audrey Lee, however, wasn’t a fan, stating that it was too firm and didn’t love that the seat doesn’t swivel. “It’s a beautiful chair, and looks much more expensive than the price suggests,” Lee says. “It’s a divisive option, but the straightforward make is something I’d prefer to have at home, when all of my distractions are nearby, and I need the chair to do the heavy-lifting of forcing me to lock in.”

Branch’s Softside chair is a fully upholstered take on their more technical office chairs. It’s still as intuitively designed as the brand’s other chairs with its adjustment points (removable arms, adjustable height, and tension recline), two back heights, and caster wheels, but think of this as your at-home companion to the Ergonomic Pro. Brighter upholstery—I’m partial to the skylight blue—also helps to cheer up a workspace suffering from too much black and grey.

The iconic Danish brand HAY has made a number of noteworthy pieces, but we’re drawn to this amply cushioned roller chair. Dating back to 2009, the 155 Task Chair has two styles: standard and soft. The latter has foam padding and batting that keeps you supported through hours-long meetings. At 20 pounds, it’s a relatively lightweight item, and it conveniently arrives fully assembled for a fuss-free setup process. Plus, the curved seat is one of several ergonomic elements. The chair has a tilting mechanism and gas lift to adjust the angle and height of the seat. This is one of many chairs in HAY’s best-selling About a Chair collection, developed by award-winning furniture designer Hee Welling.

Introduced in 2021, the Zeph Chair is a collaboration between Herman Miller and Berlin-based design firm Studio 7.5. It also went on to earn one of AD’s 2022 Cleverest Awards, with editors noting its midcentury-modern design and ergonomic form for lower back support. The kinematic mono-shell is the most striking feature, a contoured seat and back with voids for a futuristic look. “Even better, the playful chair’s seat is made of 50% post-consumer recycled content and zero fabric waste,” adds Sessums. If you anticipate spending hours upon hours in this chair, we recommend the optional seat pad and arm rests for added comfort. Another thing to feel good about? The polymer shell is easy to clean with a damp cloth, and the 12-year warranty gives you extra peace of mind about investing in a relatively splurge-y item.

Louisa Pierce and Emily Ward of AD100 firm Pierce & Ward have been trusted to design homes for celebrity clients like Dakota Johnson and Emma Roberts, and their collaboration with West Elm shows their vintage-inspired, quiet luxury aesthetic. This button-tufted, swiveling office chair will instantly ground your space. It’s sophisticated and substantial, and the adjustable height lever is located under the seat. If the in-stock upholstery isn’t for you, there are 74 options to customize your chair. So, if you’re working from your living room or the office, you should feel right at home—a concept Pierce and Ward considered while designing their firm’s new Los Angeles studio. As Ward previously shared with AD, “There’s just a different kind of energy when a workspace feels like a home.” Keep in mind this is a limited-edition product, so it’s best to nab it ASAP.

One of the newest models from Swiss furniture manufacturer Vitra, the Mynt Task Chair is a thoughtfully designed, minimalist option for a modern office. Because of the slim profile, this would work well in a home office with a versatile, space-saving desk like the Pierce Wall Desk from West Elm. The natural oak veneer backrest, armrest, and seat is our preferred colorway, but the upholstered styles provide more cushioning, thanks to the polyurethane foam and polyester fiber fill. The responsive design adjusts the seat based on your movements (a.k.a. no manual adjustments needed), and the patented tilt mechanism is hidden within the aluminum frame. Pair it with an oak-stained desk to complement your chair, while also bringing more natural texture to a home office setup.

For the midcentury aesthetes, Arhaus’s leather pieces are contemporary takes on nostalgic silhouettes. Case in point: the Kirsten Faux Leather Desk Chair, an ergonomic approach to a classic leather seat, complete with rounded edges. It can easily find a home in an earth-toned office with a walnut-stained desk, and the antique brass legs add another natural hue to the design. And while it may look like it hails from a different era, there are plenty of updated features, such as the hydraulic lift to change up the height of the seat. Four sturdy, powdercoated aluminum legs are designed to endure long days at the office. And if you’re drawn to the shape of curved back and seat, the brand’s Kirsten collection includes dining chairs and stools. We like the faux leather upholstery, but Arhaus also makes this office chair with green performance velvet and white textured performance weave if you want try other options.

Our commitment to bringing you quality seat recs is well documented, and finding an office chair that is comfortable, well-made, and easy on the eyes can make a world of difference in how you feel while you’re sitting in a seemingly endless one-hour meeting. The Shop AD team thoroughly vets items before including them in our roundups, and we test nearly everything we write about—office chairs being no exception. I, alongside our broader team of writers and editors, tested more than 30 chairs combined to pull together these rankings, with only a few making the cut in our best-of list. I’ve yet to find a stylish, non-bulky gaming chair that meets our standard, and several other generic Amazon picks just didn’t feel elevated enough to make our list of chairs that would suit a design lover—though they may tick the boxes from a purely practical standpoint. Our reviews are always thorough, in-depth, and honest, even when we’re noting how a chair may have fallen short.

Weary workers can rest assured that every pick on this list has been hand-picked and personally vetted by us. Our well-rounded list includes design head-approved picks (Herman Miller! Knoll! Steelcase!) with more approachable best-sellers on Amazon (like Branch) sprinkled in, with top priority going to picks that had a warranty of at least seven years and merged great design with adjustability and comfort.

Over the years spent testing, we’ve also delisted picks from Article, Haworth, Herman Miller, Flash Furniture, Steelcase, Flexispot, and Humanscale that either felt not ergonomic enough for an office setting or didn’t feel like the most superlative choice for their price bracket compared to their peers. The Article Svelti is armless, for example, while the Steelcase Gesture had a stiff backrest and a tedious assembly process. An older version of the Branch Ergonomic has been replaced with the brand new Branch Ergonomic Pro, which was tested by several of our editors.

Whether from the desks of the Condé Nast offices or from home setups, the Architectural Digest team has spent weeks (sometimes months or years) sitting in, working from, and recording their thoughts on the best office chairs. I am a firm believer that the chair makes the workplace, and my fellow editors agree, assuring that each of these chairs met a specific set of criteria—which I’ve outlined below—in order to pass the qualifications to be included in this article.

Delivery and assembly: Straight out the gate, did the chair arrive within the guaranteed delivery window? And if you had to assemble it, was it relatively easy to do so or did it come with a tough-to-parse manual and 100 parts?

Dimensions: Apartment dwellers know better than anyone that being conservative with floor real estate isn’t a want, but a need. That’s why our reviews provide exact measurements for the styles we tested and any notes on whether we thought a chair might not be a good fit (literally) for a modest-sized workspace.

Rating the experience: A chair that’s both easy on the eyes and on the tush is our number one priority. What was your first impression of the chair? Does the design fit a clear aesthetic? Is it meant to be ergonomic? How do the materials perform, and do they seem durable? How did you feel after a full work day and week? Does it include any fun details that may not be obvious at first glance? Our reviews were crafted to give insight on why a chair could be the right one for your 40-hour work week.

What to keep in mind: Everyone has different ideas of perfection—which is why each chair also has a section detailing what a potential buyer should keep in mind. For example, if assembly was particularly difficult, if the chair had special care instructions, and if the design seemed polarizing, we made note of all that.

Editor’s Note: We recently de-listed the Article Svelti office chair due to it being armless in favor of more supportive options.

What Features Should I Look for in an Office Chair?

Our experts—TikTok’s favorite neurosurgeon, Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT—agree that your back rest should be made from breathable material such as mesh for better air circulation, decreased perspiration, and greater comfort overall. Your seat is another important component for gluteal support that should have adequate padding consisting of dense foam or similar materials. Adjustability for different body types is crucial no matter which new chair you choose, so you can ensure your feet are positioned flat on the floor and arms set at a 90-degree angle.

Like any investment piece of furniture, you get what you pay for. There’s a lot of science that goes into crafting a comfortable and supportive office chair that you can actually be productive in. Ergonomic design, smooth movement, textiles, and manufacturing costs all combine to set the price point. Office chairs are so expensive because you’re not only investing in a chair, but also making an investment in your physical health. We spend at least eight hours a day in these seats, and they can dramatically affect our posture, joint health, and mobility. You may not notice the benefits of a great office chair, but you’ll definitely remember your discomfort in a bad one. Of course, there are budget-friendly options, like the Haworth Breck chair that we tested, which comes in above $400.

How Long do Office Chairs Typically Last?

High-quality office chairs typically last between seven and 10 years, which is why we prioritized picks that offer a lengthy warranty to cover the majority of this period. Cheaper office chairs have a much shorter lifespan, typically just a few years. Non-performance fabrics and leather seats will show their age more than performance materials that are better equipped to handle stains, scratches, and general wear and tear. You’ll know it’s time for a new seat when the customizable features—such as armrests, height, and seat position—start to wear out and aren’t as easy to adjust.

What Are the Differences Between Office Chair Styles?

Task: As the name suggests, task chairs are designed for specific tasks. Think of these chairs as short-term, minimal seating for quick bursts of work. They often have a less padded, simpler design and less support than true ergonomic office chairs that are designed for full days. Branch describes these seats as, “Task chairs embrace simplicity in their design, often characterized by a streamlined appearance. They prioritize functionality over excess features, aiming to deliver a no-frills seating solution that's easy to maneuver and adjust.” In this list, the Fritz Hansen Series 7 chair is a high-design task chair.

Executive: An executive office chair typically features a plush seat, high back, and ample spine support to keep you comfortable throughout the entire workday. You’ll find that these chairs offer more adjustment points and customization, like the 14 points on the Branch Ergonomic Pro we tested. Executive chairs come in a variety of materials and silhouettes, from Herman Miller’s signature Eames Aluminum Group chair to the brand’s more futuristic Aeron chair.

Gaming: The most specific type of office chair, gaming chairs have a very distinct shape. Usually with wide shoulders and an ultra-high back that supports your head and neck, gaming chairs prioritize lounge-style comfort without sacrificing ergonomic support. Most include a neck pillow and a lumbar pillow for additional padding and support. While the back is not as adjustable as some office chairs, gaming chairs offer additional customization points on the armrests and base.

Your office chair is just a piece of the puzzle when it comes to outfitting your WFH setup. Brands like Herman Miller, Steelcase, and Branch all offer great desks, filing cabinets, and bookcases to help fill your workspace with design-minded pieces. For those who value flexibility and ergonomic support, look to Branch for our top-tested seats and sit-to-stand desks that can withstand all-day, everyday use. For the midcentury obsessed, there’s no better place to find retro pieces than Design Within Reach. Essential brands like Eames, Knoll, and Vipp are all featured alongside some more modern favorites like Audo Copenhagen, HAY, and Tom Dixon. While we may not be able to channel the Scandinavian vacation policies, we can infuse our workspaces with more of their colorful minimalism to combat that three o’clock slump. If you prefer something more sculptural than corporate-leaning, Lulu and Georgia offers curved stone desks, upholstered seats, and plenty of desk accessories to incorporate more personality. For a full rundown of where to buy office furniture, read our guide here.

Across our vast library of home tours, we’ve noticed a few recurring characters for home offices that designers reach for again and again. Herman Miller, a favorite of our team as well, appears countless times. The retailer, having reached midcentury-modern icon status, is almost instantly recognizable. The aluminum frames, channeled leather upholstery, and wooden details elevate a home office while still providing tested ergonomic support. Jeff Goldblum’s California home boasts the brand’s Eames Aluminum Group chair, and Kevin Hart’s West Hollywood office features the Eames Executive Chair. Design Within Reach is another retailer designers frequent. Other midcentury staples can be found here too, like Knoll’s Morrison chair, the Vipp453+ Swivel Chair (which we’ve previously tested, but removed in favor of office chairs with more ergonomic features), and the Saarinen swivel chair (as seen in Margot Robbie’s production offices).

Does My Office Chair Need Lumbar Support?

Whether you’re sitting in your office chair eight hours a day or just here and there, yes, you need lumbar support. We’re all familiar with the aches that come when sleeping on a sofa for the night or after a long-haul flight, and proper back support helps to mitigate that pain and protect your spine in the process. According to our experts (Betsy Grunch, MD, FAANS, FACS and Gainesville Physical Therapy's Kristy Basinger PT, CHT, cited above), a proper-fitting desk chair is one of the cornerstones of postural health. People who sit for long hours in a poorly adjusted chair will experience neck, back, shoulder, and hip pain. This can trigger headaches, lack of concentration, and compression of the discs in the spine. Low back pain is one of the main reasons for missed days at work, so it’s essential to choose a chair that supports the spine. (It’s also not a bad idea to support your overall health and quality rest with a good mattress for back pain.)

#4806. The Courage to Question Our Own Certainty

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

There are a plethora of potentially polarizing issues these days in all aspects of our lives! It seems that we can hardly get a point of view on the table before a fellow conversationalist debunks our idea and discredits us along the way. Take your pick from a bushel full of igniting issues, whether it be global warming, wars, increasing the tax percentage for the very wealthy, or the strengths and weaknesses of our favorite political personalities; there will be no shortage of strong opinions. You can also be assured that before the full set of points of view are exposed or explored, one or more folks will have already decided what the correct point of view should be.

Our positioning and decisions on an issue seem like they happen in the blink of an eye. This instant judgement can create ill will, stress for us and the other, and can challenge or ruin long-standing relationships. Furthermore, it will likely lead to a suboptimal exploration and resolution of the salient points of view. The pivot that I would like to explore is realizing that although our interpretations and positions usually feel quite certain to us, they most likely do not represent the whole of the reality of that situation; they are a narrower, biased slice of the problem or solution.

I would like to explore what can happen when we can loosen our grip on our story/point of view, and instead consider what might ensue if we instead question our own certainty. This, of course, would require slowing down enough to really listen first and then explore the fuller reality of the situation together; then, with skillful listening and openness to other ways of thinking, we can have a meaningful and civil dialogue.

We seem to be experiencing a plethora of fractured conversations, competing accounts of the truth, information overload, and fear about the future, all of which are leading to what we might call “contemporary exhaustion.” And if the impact of this on us personally wasn’t enough, the relational tension as well as the societal and political challenges are at an all-time high. It is so much more likely that answers to our difficult questions will land somewhere in the middle of the two opposing extremes being debated, or in a yet-to-be-discovered “third alternative” idea that cannot possibly be uncovered because of the anger, tension, and lack of listening in the interchange. Just to ground this idea in one statistic: the American Psychological Association's Stress in America survey, "A Crisis of Connection," reported that 62% of adults considered societal divisions a significant stressor in their lives.

If you are willing to have the “courage to suspend the certainty” of your initial interpretation and allow for more information, thoughts, and feelings to emerge between you and another, amazing things can happen. Try following a simple practice of what I will call “thoughtful receptivity” using these 4 steps. Imagine that, before you know it, you are in a polarizing conversation with challenging points of view and heated feelings emerging. Each side draws his/her sword, and the point-counterpoint debate begins. You have enough presence to realize you are in the battle, and it likely will not end well. You feel triggered and notice the same for the other person. You remember this practice and do the following:

We all have the tendency to confuse the story we have crafted and are trying to tell with the whole truth about a situation. Perhaps a better way to proceed is to remain open to what we have not yet explored or understood, remain open to another way of thinking about a situation, and remain open to the other person. If we could find the grace to do so, we might learn to see and understand more deeply before we judge. All of this ultimately requires that we develop the courage to question our own certainty. If we could do so, it is very likely that our world would become a much better, kinder place to live and thrive.

American Psychological Association. (2025). Stress in America 2025: A crisis of connection. https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/stress-in-america/2025

#4800. Should Scientists Ignore Philosophers of Science?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

The eminent evolutionary biologist and modeller John Maynard Smith was once asked about Karl Popper and the philosophy of science. His answer was not flattering. His impression was that scientists who take the philosophy of science seriously, and allow their research to be influenced by philosophical preconceptions, are "far more likely to do themselves harm than good". He loved reading philosophy of science and was always ready to argue about it, he added, but he did not believe that one should allow oneself to be influenced by it when actually thinking about science.

This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic. These are quite radical words, and though Maynard Smith's generalisation is untenable, there is an important insight to be extracted.

If modellers approach the philosophical literature on models with the goal of figuring out what models are and what a good model is, they might easily find themselves lured into naive monistic views of models that fail to represent the full epistemic richness of modelling practices, thereby turning them into worse scientists than they could have otherwise been.

This could happen in several ways. For instance, models with epistemic functions not recognised by narrow monist accounts might be discarded. Consider, for example, models with weak predictive power, but great generality and insight into complex systems.

Perhaps Maynard Smith's worry is most strongly illustrated in economics, where Milton Friedman and Karl Popper are taken to have the "last word" in any methodological debate, and are frequently invoked to both defend and criticise the work of modellers. They are perhaps paradigm cases of monist thinking. Friedman argued that the only relevant desideratum in science concerns predictive power, while Popper argued that what matters is falsifiability.

These accounts of science have received extensive criticism over the last decades. Indeed, the philosopher Alex Rosenberg argued that Friedman's naive picture single-handedly justified the existence of philosophy of economics as a distinct profession. Economists, however, are unlikely to read much if any work on methodology beyond Friedman and Popper. As the economist Dani Rodrik notes, economic methodology is relegated to specialised journals and, more importantly, is not really being taught in graduate school.

The result is that economists seem to believe that their science operates according to a simple form of falsificationism, a picture of science that, most contemporary philosophers of science would agree, both misrepresents scientific practice and provides the wrong ideal of how science ought to function.

The obvious counter to Maynard Smith's concern is that it is not an argument against the philosophy of science, but rather against bad philosophy of science, which limits, rather than fosters, insights into the richness of the epistemic tools available to scientists.

Philosophers are not innocent here. Some debates in the philosophy of science rest on such monist motivations to seek univocal accounts of laws, explanation, species, functions, preferences, and many more. As Peter Godfrey-Smith emphasised, one of the hazards of philosophy is the temptation to come up with theories that are "too broad and sweeping". This hazard has not been avoided in the philosophical literature on models. Many philosophers of science seem to be under the impression that once we figure out what "models" are and how they work, we can finally get a handle on all the other pressing questions in the philosophy of science. I argue that this way of thinking about models is grounded in a mistake.

A philosophy of science worth reading takes the plurality, diversity, and richness of models and modelling practices seriously. It does not hand scientists a single criterion for good science.

Economists, Rodrik argues, need a better story about the kind of science they practise, and some economists have recently engaged with philosophical questions themselves, seeking contact with philosophers of economics in the process. Philosophers of science, in turn, should turn more of their attention toward both the social sciences and the philosophy of the social sciences. Their lack of engagement with this rich literature is a historical omission that may have provided a misguided understanding of how science works.

Should scientists ignore philosophers? They should ignore those who tell them that there is only one way of doing science well.

Veit, W. (2019). Model Pluralism. Philosophy of the Social Sciences, 50(2), 91–114. https://doi.org/10.1177/0048393119894897 [Download]

Friedman, M. (1953). The Methodology of Positive Economics. In Essays in Positive Economics, 3–43. University of Chicago Press.

Godfrey-Smith, P. (2003). Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science. University of Chicago Press.

Maynard Smith, J. (1997). Interview by Richard Dawkins. Web of Stories. https://www.webofstories.com/play/john.maynard.smith/99

Popper, K. (1959). The Logic of Scientific Discovery. Routledge.

Rodrik, D. (2015). Economics Rules: Why Economics Works, When It Fails, and How to Tell the Difference. Oxford University Press.

Rosenberg, A. (2009). If Economics Is a Science, What Kind of a Science Is It? In H. Kincaid and D. Ross (eds), The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Economics, 55–67. Oxford University Press.

The Black Friday furniture deals are going strong, and we’ve rounded up a hearty list of discounts that are so tasty they may just overshadow grandma’s famous pumpkin pie leftovers. No matter where you lie on the design spectrum—coastal, midcentury, farmhouse—there’s an upgrade for you at a price that’s more than palatable. Some of our favorite brands have rolled out discounts on living room furniture, bedroom sets, and statement pieces that have absolutely no business being in our shopping cart but somehow end up there anyway. Considering how quickly foundational pieces like a new sofa, bed frame, or dresser can gobble up a decorating budget, we’re certainly not complaining.

We’ve highlighted the brands offering big deals for you to take advantage of. So fret not—that statement area rug or lovely sectional sofa you were hoping to score for a fraction of the price is well within reach! Bookmark this page, we’ll be updating it as more Black Friday furniture deals go live.

There comes a hellish time in all lives where it becomes clear the living room needs a bit of a refresh—a potentially pricey undertaking. The good news is that if we’re tactful about it, any upgrades can be up to 70% off thanks to Black Friday sales. In search of a new sectional? We’ve tested them extensively. Need a good reading chair to tie it altogether? We’ve tested those, too. We have guides to consoles, coffee tables, a hefty piece on Black Friday rug sales. Basically, whatever you need—we’ve got some recommendations. Here’s our best-of list for high-quality, stylish pieces at a fraction of their price.

Not everyone has the time to wait for a solid oak heirloom to fall into their lap, and these dignified pieces are worthwhile alternatives. Whether you have a dedicated dining room (you lucky dog), or a tiny kitchen that needs to pull double duty, the right dining table for you is on mega sale so you can host big parties at home regardless of space constraints. Our favorite deal? An extra 25% off the Elle dining table from Lulu & Georgia makes it an even better buy.

There’s something you should probably know about us: We love sleep. So much so that we've tested upwards of 30 mattresses and sleep-related products, all in the name of making sure you have recommendations you can rely on. Black Friday is very much the time to invest in a mattress at a discounted price if you're looking to enter the new year with a better sleep report from your smartwatch, but we don’t think you should neglect the remainder of your bedroom. With that in mind, we’ve rounded up a few great deals on bed frames, dressers, nightstands, and even a few bedding deals to have you waking up on the right side of the bed in 2027.

While the weather outside is frightful, the deals on outdoor furniture are just the opposite. One of our favorite outdoor brands, Neighbor, has slashed 15% sitewide, so teak and wicker finds are now within budget’s reach. Outer is also offering 30% on its full teak sets, outdoor umbrellas, fire pit setups, and you can even score additional patio pieces for free at a certain purchase point. One of our favorite gifting hubs, Anthropologie, also stocks a surprisingly robust assortment of furniture and decor. If you’ve got a robust collection of tchotchkes that deserve their own moment, the Fern storage cabinet is the perfect way to help them shine.

Makers of American classics, Arhaus is running discounts across all of their departments. Whether you're looking for holiday decor or a hefty sectional, Arhaus has got a sale going. Contributor Lila Allen instantly fell in love with her Kipton sofa, “The combo of soft curves and clean and modern lines make this a really versatile piece,” Lila said. “My apartment is eclectic, and it fit right in with our existing decor—so consider this a solid example of transitional style. Note: You need a mattress in your cart for the discount to apply. And if a bedroom overhaul is in the cards, Saatva’s upholstered Halle storage platform bed offers a discreet place to stash extra bedding totally out of sight.

A little coastal influence can go a long way, even if the nearest beach is blanketed in snow during the off-season. Serena & Lily is currently hosting The Sale of the Year, with up to 50% off furniture, mirrors, and lighting, plus discounts across nearly every other product category. It’s a chance to bring the brand’s breezy, tailored aesthetic home in time for the holidays. We’re particularly fond of its outdoor lineup, including the Pacifica Sofa, which AD contributor Blake Bakkila put to the test for more than three years at her Newport Beach home. Despite its exposure to coastal moisture, she reported no fading, warping, or damage, and gave the sofa an overall A rating. For an indoor refresh, the Carter counter stool brings the brand’s signature natural texture into the kitchen.

These contemporary heirlooms are more likely to be passed down from one generation to the next than they are to go out of style, so these prices are practically a steal.

During its Black Friday sale, West Elm is offering up to 70% off plus an extra 20% off select styles. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert tested the queen-size version in dark olive performance velvet and called it “the softest, cushiest couch in my house.” Another standout from the sale is the midcentury five-drawer dresser, a handsome storage solution narrow enough for smaller bedrooms and cozy apartments. Equally impressive deals can be found on accent chairs, dining tables, and some of the brand’s bestsellers.

In case you need direction, contributor Rachel Kalichman called Interior Define’s Gaby sectional “an elegant and neutral piece that can fit any type of decor style.”

#4798. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4797. Is Conspiracy Thinking in the Person or the Place?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Here are three statements. How much do you agree with each?

Food should be chosen based on each person's blood group.

Evidence of alien contact is being concealed from the public.

These seem to have little in common, but people who agree with one tend to agree with the others (Lobato and colleagues, 2014).

All three statements come from questionnaires that measure what researchers call epistemically suspect beliefs: confident claims about how the world works that go beyond, or against, the available evidence.

Because these beliefs hang together so well, many researchers treat them as something close to a personality trait, a stable way of seeing things. Others see them as a response to the world. Conspiracy theories, for example, tend to spread during periods of social crisis (van Prooijen and Douglas, 2017).

If these beliefs are traits, they should stay roughly the same from year to year, regardless of what happens around a person. A response to the world would instead rise and fall as people’s view of that world changes. Most studies cannot tell which is true, because they measure people only once.

In a paper just published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, my colleagues and I tested the two views (Alper and colleagues, 2026). The project, led by Sinan Alper of Yaşar University. was funded by TÜBİTAK, Türkiye's national science agency.

We surveyed the same adults in Türkiye and the United Kingdom five times, once every six months. At the start, 2,077 people participated in Türkiye and 959 in the UK. Each time, they reported these beliefs and rated corruption among public officials, business executives, and the media, as well as other attitudes.

The two countries differ sharply on corruption. On Transparency International’s (2026) Corruption Perceptions Index, the UK ranks 20th of 182 countries, and Türkiye ranks 124th.

On average, the beliefs declined slightly over the two years, except for conspiracy belief in Türkiye, which showed no clear change. I wouldn't read much into this, since answering the same questions repeatedly can itself lower scores. What struck me more was how tightly linked the three beliefs were. At the start, the correlations between them were strong, ranging from .65 to .86. Change was linked even more tightly. When a person’s belief in the paranormal fell, their belief in pseudoscience and conspiracy theories tended to fall with it.

One possibility is that all three reflect a single underlying tendency. Simpler explanations, such as people answering the survey less carefully over time, cannot yet be ruled out. Either way, much of the change is shared, but not all of it.

In Türkiye, people who saw more corruption over the past two years also became more open to conspiracy theories. Their paranormal and pseudoscientific beliefs did not follow. In the UK, we found no such link.

This may seem to clash with the previous section, and in part it does. Most of the change in these beliefs is shared, but each may keep some room to move on its own. In Türkiye, corruption may have tracked the portion attributable to conspiracy beliefs alone. It makes sense that belief in conspiracy was the one to move. A conspiracy theory claims that powerful people are secretly working together for their own gain. Corruption is often a true version of that story. Black cats and blood-type diets have nothing to do with it.

At the start of the study, though, the link between perceived corruption and conspiracy belief was about twice as strong in the UK (r = .61) as in Türkiye (r = .32). The difference may come down to how common corruption is. Where it is relatively rare, seeing it everywhere may say more about the person than about the country and may function as a stable trait. Where corruption is widespread and changing, people’s sense of it may follow those changes, and conspiracy beliefs may shift accordingly.

Our answer is both. These beliefs are steady and hang together, but they can still change.

Some factors seem to set a person’s starting point. People higher in authoritarianism, who value discipline and following leaders in unity, endorsed all three kinds of beliefs more in both countries. But changes in authoritarianism did not track changes in belief. Perceived corruption works differently, and whether it moves these beliefs seems to depend on where you live.

This fits earlier work. Conspiracy beliefs are more common in countries with widespread corruption and in less stable societies, where education offers less protection against them (Alper, 2023). In another study I coauthored, education was also less tied to trust in science in highly corrupt countries (Alper and colleagues, 2024). In such places, people might learn to distrust authority from experience.

When someone you know shares a conspiracy theory, ask two questions. Is this how they see everything, from health advice to the evening news? Or is it a response to something they have watched go wrong? The first kind of belief tends to change slowly. The second should be taken seriously, because sometimes suspicion points at something real.

Careful thinking still matters. In a recent experiment, my colleagues and I found that training designed to encourage reflection lowered conspiracy beliefs (Bayrak and colleagues, 2025). But when institutions keep giving people reasons to be suspicious, better thinking can only do so much. I guess that in some places the best answer to conspiracy thinking is institutions that give people less to suspect. Survey data like ours cannot settle that.

Sinan Alper and I have begun to test it experimentally. In two preregistered studies with nationally representative US samples, we described an unnamed US state or a fictional country as either highly corrupt or very clean (Alper and Yilmaz, 2026).

People found conspiracy claims about the corrupt place far more believable, and this was most closely tied to a sense that resources were being shared unfairly. The paper is still under peer review, and I will write about it once it is done.

Alper, S. (2023). There are higher levels of conspiracy beliefs in more corrupt countries. European Journal of Social Psychology, 53(3), 503–517. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.2919

Alper, S., Konukoglu, K., Bayrak, F., Yener, C., Bagci, E. S., Dogruyol, B., & Yilmaz, O. (2026). Stable worldviews or context-sensitive systems? Longitudinal evidence on the development of epistemically suspect beliefs across two sociopolitical contexts. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672261463908

Alper, S., Yelbuz, B. E., Akkurt, S. B., & Yilmaz, O. (2024). The positive association of education with the trust in science and scientists is weaker in highly corrupt countries. Public Understanding of Science, 33(1), 2–19. https://doi.org/10.1177/09636625231176935

Alper, S., & Yilmaz, O. (2026, June 11). Corruption cues increase conspiracy beliefs: the central role of perceived distributive fairness. Retrieved from osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/jfr4n_v1

Bayrak, F., Sümer, V., Dogruyol, B., Saribay, S. A., Alper, S., Isler, O., & Yilmaz, O. (2025). Reflection predicts and leads to decreased conspiracy belief. Cognition, 258, 106085. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2025.106085

Lobato, E., Mendoza, J., Sims, V., & Chin, M. (2014). Examining the relationship between conspiracy theories, paranormal beliefs, and pseudoscience acceptance among a university population. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 28(5), 617–625. https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.3042

Transparency International. (2026). Corruption Perceptions Index 2025. https://www.transparency.org/en/cpi/2025

van Prooijen, J.-W., & Douglas, K. M. (2017). Conspiracy theories as part of history: The role of societal crisis situations. Memory Studies, 10(3), 323–333. https://doi.org/10.1177/1750698017701615

#4796. Cole Haan Has the Most Comfortable Dress Shoes on Sale for Black Friday

We’re seeing jaw-dropping deals up to 68% off.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

BLACK FRIDAY IS officially here, and Cole Haan is rolling out some pretty sweet deals with markdowns up to 68 percent off select styles on the brand’s website and Amazon. This is the time of year when I get dressed up the most—layering up for the cold office commutes and getting ready for holiday gatherings, so I’m going to need comfortable dress shoes to help me get through it all. That’s why Cole Haan has become one of my go-to destinations for just that. The brand has a knack for combining classic, polished styles with the level of comfort you’d expect from your favorite sneakers. Everything from dressy oxfords to every day dress sneakers that can easily pull double duty is seeing a price drop. It’s not everyday these shoes receive a markdown, so I wouldn’t bank on your size still being available as the hours go on.

Cole Haan ØriginalGrand Horizon Wingtip Oxfords

Cole Haan 2.ZERØGRAND Laser Wingtip Oxfords

Cole Haan GrandPrø SkyWeave Low-Profile Sneakers

Cole Haan Grand Crosscourt Daily Court Sneakers

One of the biggest discounts is the 2.ZERØGRAND Laser Wingtip Oxford, marked down 58 percent. It’s like a mashup of an athletic sneaker and a traditional dress shoe. The nubuck and polyester upper features a laser-cut wingtip pattern that puts a modern twist on classic broguing, while the lightweight sole keeps things from feeling too stiff or clunky. I’ve found that the Grandfoam—the brand’s proprietary cushioning—has a slightly squishy feel underfoot, but in a good way. There’s enough give to keep my feet comfortable without making the shoe feel unstable. Plus, the hybrid design looks just as good with chinos as it does with dress pants.

For something a little more laid-back, check out the Grand Atlantic Sneaker at 44 percent off. It has that clean, tennis-inspired look that plays well with relaxed, business-casual outfits or straight-leg jeans and a sweater. What really sells me is how lightweight it feels. There’s a rubber sole underneath, but I barely notice it when I’m walking on these New York City sidewalks that aren’t exactly forgiving. I always throw this sneaker on for our photo shoot days that tend to go over eight hours.

#4794. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#4791. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4790. What China Taught Me About America's Rambunctious Streak

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

I've long wondered whether a rambunctious toddler is more likely to develop a balanced temperament than a reticent tike. Is a quiet kid more likely to learn boldness than a bold child is to learn when to shut up?

I bring that up because, having just visited China, I've been thinking about the trajectories of our almost opposite nations.

The Chinese are a much more cooperative population than we are. It shows up even in the fluid dynamics of the society.

I spent a lot of time walking through non-touristy streets. That's not enough to make me an expert, but I did form impressions. People flow around each other more fluidly than they do here. They're not distracted by each other. They don't nod or look each other in the eye. They simply assume each other. There seems to be no stigma in being glued to a phone.

They're less thirsty for attention. They aren't busy reassuring each other or trying to stand out. They strain less to look and feel exceptional. There were plenty of stylish young people, but not to the extent we see here. Even the ads are less glam.

It stands to reason. This is a huge, dense urban population whose parents and grandparents, a generation or two ago, were mostly peasants. Their society was shaped by Confucianism 2,500 years ago, a philosophy that is more about etiquette than anything else, at least in its popular form.

Yes, the Chinese have at times gone terribly off the rails. Indonesia also struck me as an extraordinarily tolerant society, yet 60 years ago anti-Communists there slaughtered over a million people. Societies can change. But today China is a mild child. We're the thirsty, intense, fanatical, exceptionalist, rambunctious one.

We distract ourselves with obscene amounts of self-flattery and pandering in commerce and politics. The midterms alone cost 12 billion dollars. All that pandering and flattery doesn't make us wiser. It makes us more anxious and delusional.

We've just about used up the earth's carrying capacity for self-flattering nonsense. Meanwhile, the demand for flattery and pandering is only getting worse.

In China, there's so little of it, at least so far. That could change, as it did in Indonesia after I visited eight years ago, with the rise of Islamic fundamentalism.

China doesn't go through the motions of national elections. It's one-party rule, with no pandering and a focus on practical welfare that, on my visit, went far beyond what we see here. They plan to double their train lines by 2035. There's practically no theft in the city center, and the cameras are everywhere, so you'd get caught and punished. China's Gini coefficient, a measure of wealth inequality, is around 35. Ours is about ten points higher.

On my two trips there, I met only one Christian. It's an atheist country, and you can't talk about the supernatural as real. There's none of our jersey-wearing, lifestyle-brand supernaturalist grandstanding and infighting.

People grumble about the lack of freedom of speech, but they can grumble without looking over their shoulders. At Peking University, built on the land of the emperor's Summer Palace and just a few blocks from the government center, a professor told me that, paradoxically, they have more freedom of speech there. In distant cities, you have to attend a Communist Party meeting every two weeks. At the university, you just fill out minutes. There are limits, though. You can't talk casually about Mao on social media, and you can't call him a dictator. They're trying to put the violence of the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution behind them, along with the poverty. In 1976, China's average income was a third of Sub-Saharan Africa's. They've come a long way. Maybe they'll keep going.

If you're not watching China, you should be. Odds are they will surpass us, and Pax Americana will give way to Pax Sinica. Since I study American fanaticism, I could get a distorted view of humankind. China makes me think humankind might pull off some kind of harmony. It fills me with optimism about human potential.

And maybe we'll learn from China's success. Maybe the rambunctious child will learn to chill out. We had better.

Maybe we'll converge on some mix of reticent and rambunctious that makes humankind survivable.

#4788. Huawei set to challenge Tesla Powerwall with new, 20 kW home battery

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! If you’re shopping for a Tesla Powerwall alternative that won’t help fund the absolute worst people in politics, there are a number of great home battery systems on the market that can deliver backup power, store your solar energy, and keep your home running when the grid goes down.
