#4787. 10 Best Sectional Sofas That Are Actually Stylish, Tested (2026)

As former AD editor Benjamin Reynaert puts it, sectionals allow for “a level of customization akin to bespoke furniture, but without the high costs that come with building a piece from the ground—or sofa leg—up.” Sectionals, more than standard sofas, have a kind of chameleonic style that can adapt just as easily to a basement movie room or the family den. But deciding between the right sectional versus a regular old sofa can still be tough.

If you’re worried that sectionals can lean a bit stodgy or will have trouble squeezing into tight spaces, we’re here to ease your mind with some of our team’s first-hand findings from years of sitting, napping, and binge-watching on the best sectional sofas around. Whether you’re looking for a chaise to stretch out on or a corner piece to anchor your media room, there’s a versatile silhouette just waiting to be brought home. Shop our favorite plush, sculptural picks and sleek, midcentury classics below.

Benchmade doesn’t stop at sending fabric swatches. The company will send you a true-to-size printouts so you know exactly what you’re getting, among more than 125 material and fabric combos of your choosing. That way, you can go beyond visualizing how the Modern Vintage sofa will fit in your space. The brand’s recently launched Vintage collection is for those of us who pine for retro designs but don’t want to spend the hours thumbing through Facebook Marketplace for a secondhand option. The line offers midcentury modern-inspired designs in patterned prints from the likes of Kravet and textile house Pollack. Contributor Noah Kaufman chose the plaid upholstery seen here from Pollack (which is available later this month) and a silhouette with sled legs to fit with his Victorian home’s aesthetic. “In a home with a more midcentury aesthetic, or one that uses more pronounced colors and patterns, it would fit right in,” Kaufman says, noting that the sofa reminds him of the couch in his childhood home.

Despite being known for budget-friendly bamboo and breezy linen bedding, Quince’s recent foray into furniture met our team with equal parts enthusiasm and curiosity. Handmade in North Carolina, where some of the best American furniture hails from, the pieces are designed to be home staples with a timeless aesthetic and for those who aren’t willing to shell out five figures for a sectional. After years spent with a well-loved, second-hand grey sofa, audience development manager Emma Tubbs knew it was time for an upgrade. Enter: Quince’s modern silhouette, the Ashford Deep Seat Chaise Sectional in the performance velvet. “When I found this Quince piece, I was immediately drawn to the gorgeous, deep brown velvet, but the deep seat is really what sold me,” she says. “I love being able to cozy up and lie down on a couch, and in my opinion, there's nothing worse than a narrow sectional.” With a 28-inch seat depth and cushions filled with high-density foam and a feather/down blend, this sofa is meant for all-day comfort. Her one critique: Tubbs notes that while the seat is supportive and plush, the back cushions easily lose their shape and need fluffing after every nap. That said, “the overall construction feels solid and well-made, and I’ve already taken many naps on the couch and woken up refreshed and without any back pain,” she says.

Velvet isn’t always the right upholstery choice for those looking for durability, but the brand’s performance velvet easily withstands spills and pets, needing just a spot clean when you notice a stain. Overall, Tubbs notes that it’s great for game nights just as it is for sick days and rainy weekends spent reading indoors. Even her dog gives it the thumbs up: “While we’re trying to limit our 80-pound very hairy German Shepherd’s access to the new couch, it does warm my heart that the couch can comfortably accommodate all three of us sprawled out.”

Castlery’s Hamilton sectional has a classic design with its tapered arms and boxy shape, and it also happens to be a sleeper sofa. Suiting a more modern or traditional aesthetic, the sectional keeps its structure while still being a crazy comfortable place to lounge around. “My partner and I are true couch people and love to lie around, so getting another sectional was the obvious choice,” says contributor Susie Plotkin. Plotkin goes on to describe this couch as wildly comfortable, and having the kind of silhouette that makes her living room look more polished than it is. It won’t be your living room’s signature piece of decor, but for those looking for a sectional that can easily adapt to their ever-evolving design style, the Hamilton might be for you.

The perk of having a sleeper sofa and a sectional in one is that there is plenty of room to spread out. And for those short on closet space, the chaise lifts up to reveal a storage compartment underneath. But unlike other jack-of-all-trades furniture pieces, this one delivers in just two boxes. Plotkin opted for white-glove delivery, and the entire couch was assembled and ready for a movie night in under an hour.

Like most sleepers, the built-in, memory foam mattress may not compare to your plush bed setup, but Plotkin insists that guests have touted the Hamilton’s comfort, night after night. “We’ve already had people sleep on both the pull-out mattress and directly on the chaise; both got glowing reviews,” she says. “The middle seat is a hair stiffer than the others because of the pullout mattress, but even that is very lounge-able. It feels well-made and durable, and because the high-density memory foam cushions retain their shape, the couch doesn’t sag.” Overall, Plotkin is extremely pleased with her sectional, especially the way it's held up against her two very rambunctious kittens (and their claws). The performance upholstery is stain-resistant and has a subtle texture that adds depth to the otherwise all-white look. Since she doesn’t have a guest room, she was looking for a versatile piece—“not just any sleeper sofa, though, a seating unicorn: a stylish, comfortable, non-bulky sleeper sectional” for her space. “It didn’t even occur to me to look for storage—I was already being greedy with my requirements, so when I found the Hamilton, it skyrocketed to the top of the shortlist,” Plotkin adds.

The Burrow is a family-friendly addition to your living spaces no matter what kind of square footage you’re working with. This three-piece sectional that’s just slightly larger than a loveseat is especially accommodating for smaller layouts and thoughtfully designed with the flexibility to tack on more seating (an ottoman, chaise, or extension here or there) as your family or space changes. The sofa’s stain-resistant upholstery, solid plywood frame, and CertiPUR-US–certified foam base also ensures lasting durability and high-quality comfort. The brand also offers a one-year warranty to give you a bit more peace of mind.

Contributor David Kaufman placed it an entryway area of his home and called it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.” He noted that it falls on the firmer end, but vouches that it’s still a comfy crowd-pleaser among the family. “It’s especially well sized for the twins to curl up in with a friend.”

The Arhaus Coburn reclining sectional is a blocky, yet modernized option (we love the exaggerated seams) for anyone looking for a comfortable recliner that’s trimmed of all the bulk of the Lay-Z-Boys from the early aughts. “The couch is exceptionally comfortable and plush, especially when you use the reclining feature,” says AD contributor Blake Bakkila, who cautions that when you’re not using it in recliner mode, it doesn’t provide as much shoulder or neck support. Another perk of the sofa is its kid-friendly surface, put to the test by Bakkila’s toddler. “The kitchen (and his beloved berries) are a quick sprint from the couch, and we’ve never noticed any stains,” Bakkila adds. It does need ample inches of clearance at the back in order to recline, so it would be better suited for floating furniture layouts rather than a room where it would need to be placed against a wall. Note that this sofa also needs to be plugged into a power source or equipped with battery packs to use the reclining features.

Thuma made a name for themselves with easy-to-build bed frames which lock into place via well-crafted Japanese joinery, though they quickly followed that up with bedroom furniture like nightstands and other modular shelving arrangements. Their most recent launches have positioned Thuma as a brand to know for beautiful furnishings in every room of the house, starting with their new modular sofas. Enhanced with additional lumber support and enforced with liquid-coated steel, these pieces are sturdy and also elegant, with commerce partnerships manager Evan Russum giving them top marks for style and design alone.

“This couch stood out to me because it avoids the bulky, overstuffed look a lot of sectionals lean into,” Russum says. “Instead, it feels streamlined and modern, with modular pieces that clip together in a seamless way that echoes the bed frame’s design ethos.” He noted that there is plenty of room to sprawl out for his lanky 6’5 frame and that despite its delicate ivory color, the couch hasn’t seen any scratches from his cat, snags, or noticeable wear from daily use.

Interior Define’s Sloan sectional offers more customization options than the traditional furniture brand. Choose from dozens of upholstery materials (and colors!), various seat depths, cushion fills, and even leg styles. The personalization is largely why contributor Malia Griggs chose this sofa for her living room. “I really do love this couch. If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space (and even with cats),” she says. Having stretched out on the chaise for movie nights, naps, and even one full night, Griggs touts the sofa’s firm yet cozy seat and durable upholstery.

Even with two rambunctious cats, the sofa has held up against spills, stains, claws, and even one poorly timed hairball. “The sectional has held up surprisingly well against their havoc—wrestling on the chaise, treating its sides like a scratching post, and near-constant shedding absolutely everywhere,” Griggs elaborates. She also says that a soft-bristle brush helps maintain the velvet texture and disguises any aggressively clawed areas. “While I wouldn’t call velvet a low-maintenance upholstery choice (it definitely attracts lint and pet hair), it has performed better than I expected,” she says. “Velvet has a short, dense pile that doesn’t snag the same way as my previous chenille sofa—so even when my cats do go to town with their claws, the fabric doesn’t show damage as obviously.”

“We were inspired to create 7th Avenue to solve for a frustration we kept hearing from customers: Finding a sofa that was both beautifully designed and genuinely practical for everyday living was surprisingly difficult,” the brand’s co-founder and CEO Billy Shaw previously told AD. The result is ultra-modular pieces like this chaise sectional, complete with water-repellent and stain-resistant fabric upholstery that are removable and washable (and replaceable if you ever want to mix it up).

Similar to the chaise sectional, this sectional sofa from 7th Avenue promises modularity and water-resistant and stain-repellent properties. The construction is modular, of course, but contributor Meg Kernahan explains how the overall look can coordinate with virtually any interior design. “This sectional has a very versatile look that can work with many different styles,” she shares in her review. “The sleek, no-frills design makes it a perfect backdrop for other elements in the room to stand out. My style leans organic modern with a touch of midcentury, and it blends with my aesthetic well.” Kernahan selected a chocolate brown color, in the hopes that the dark hue and stain-resistant fabric could conceal any marks left behind by her two young kids and dog. She notes that while it’s not completely water-resistant, it can easily repel a splash of water, and that it’s easy to remove the cushion covers and throw them in the wash.

Kernahan calls this couch “incredibly comfy” and says her family has taken several naps on it. “My husband and I can each lie down on either side of the couch at the same time without having to drape our legs over each other (we’re both about 5' 8"), so there is plenty of room to sprawl out and get comfortable,” she says. “It’s notably deep enough for a full night’s sleep (or a solid nap), especially with the back cushions removed.” And after a month of testing (and sleeping) on it, she hasn’t noticed any sagging.

Comfort and natural materials are top priorities for Sixpenny, which rebranded in 2020 to develop eco-friendly pieces with slipcover upholstery. Their feather down is ethically sourced, and the down alternative fill is made with vegan poly fibers. Our team has tested dozens of sectionals, but contributor Zoë Sessums argues this might be the comfiest she’s ever tried. “You can really sink into the seats, yet the cushion filling bounces right back,” she writes in her review. “It feels durable and well made, especially all the stitching on the slipcovers.”

Two years after bringing it home, Sessums says “all the cushions still have so much oomph” and continue to feel supportive—even after cats, dogs, small children, and tall overnight guests have all comfortably used this couch, without causing any damage. “This sofa feels nearly indestructible!” Sessums adds. Even more, her guests often ask if she purchased a new couch because she’s rearranged the units to create different configurations over the years. “Currently, I have the sofa set up as a small sofa and two chairs,” she says. “It’s a nice way to refresh your space while being less wasteful. I sometimes wish the depth was slightly shorter since my house isn’t very big, but overall it works.”

Pottery Barn has been a trusted source for high-quality furniture for decades, so it’s no wonder they make one of the most comfortable—and dare we say “dreamiest”—sectionals. “The level of comfort that this couch possesses is the stuff of legend,” writes contributor Jaha Nailah Avery in her review. “It’s probably the most comfortable couch I have ever had the pleasure of sitting on. It’s constructed so well, and you can definitely tell that it’s made from premium materials.”

True to its name, the Dream is a standard product with several customizations: two widths, an optional storage ottoman, and 80 colorways to choose from. Avery selected the wider version, and says it fits perfectly in her single-family home with a large living room. “At 172 inches wide, 86 inches deep, and 34 inches high, it is quite long, but it fills the space in a way that makes everything a little more cozy,” she explains. “I also love that you can customize its size. You can pop out one or two of the middle sections to make it smaller, or move the ottoman piece to another section.” Her dog Fievel gives a rave review, too, since the upholstery is gentle on his sensitive skin and easy to vacuum or lint roll his hair.

There are many factors we considered in each of our reviews to give you the insight you need to select the best sectional sofa for your home, including:

Ordering and customization process: Shallow seats or deep seats, armrests or armless, right-facing chaise or left-facing chaise, down seat cushions or foam cushioning, upholstery or leather, L-shape or U-shape—each of the sectionals we tested has possibilities. We also documented the lead times and expected delivery timelines for each model.

Couch delivery and assembly: Curbside or white-glove, fully assembled or DIY. And, if DIY, how many pieces did the sofa arrive in and how difficult was the assembly?

After installation: Here we asked some tough functionality questions of each sectional: Is it practical for a modern home? Is the couch kid- and/or pet-friendly? What are the care and cleaning instructions? And did it look better IRL than in the photos?

Durability and longevity: When possible, we followed up with testers to see if they still stood by their original reviews months or years down the line.

We updated this story for Seat Week 2025 with couches that AD staffers and contributors spent the summer vetting, including a new reclining sofa. Above all else, we prioritized picks during testing that were stylish, comfortable, reasonably easy to assemble, and durable enough not to stain or tear even when pets and children are present. Only picks that earned at least a B grade in our testing (which was appointed according to the factors outlined above) made the cut. Over the last successive updates, we’ve delisted picks from Lovesac and Sundays that felt less elevated than their peers for the price point. Meanwhile, a best-selling style from Albany Park that we tested has been retired by the brand as of 2026.

Of course, our homes and apartments can only fit so much seating, so we added a section of runner-up styles that we hope will round out your search for a beautiful, comfortable sofa, no matter what your budget may be. We haven’t tested these models firsthand, but we made sure to choose design-forward styles that are sold at reliable retailers. Most even include customer reviews that offer a glimpse at how these sectionals would hold up in your own home.

Deciding what sectional shape you’re in the market for will help you streamline your decision making. Take into account exactly how much square footage you have to fill, along with what kind of space it will occupy (a family-friendly space with lots of foot traffic will require different kinds of materials than a rarely used guest room, for example).

L-Shaped Sectional: Arguably the most traditional sectional shape, and the one you’ll come across most on this list, L-shaped sectionals are suitable for just about any space. They’re space maximizers—snugly fitting into corner areas and making the most out of your square footage. They also create a shape that can be corralled around a few accent chairs or a statement-making armchair (something like an Eames lounger). If you’re looking for styling inspiration, we’d point you in the direction of this Parisian apartment which coordinates the sectional and wall color to create the illusion of a bigger room, or this Gramercy Park apartment where a sectional sits back in an otherwise open layout.

U-Shaped Sectional: U-shaped sectionals are ideal for larger families looking for lots of seating as well as the perpetual hosts and hostesses, who want party guests to have a spot to kick back. For true U-shape inspiration, look to Stacey Bendet’s Upper West Side abode, where a green velvet U-shape sectional serves as the centerpiece in the designer’s colorful living room.

Curved Sectional: A cousin of the L-shaped and U-shaped sectional, the curved sectional isn’t bound by static lines. At times it takes on a true "U" design, while we’ve also seen configurations take on a snake-like S-shape. Like an L-shaped sectional, some curved sectionals work nicely in corner spots like this one in Pierre Yovanovitch’s Paris office. Curved sofas and sectionals are also unique because they don't necessarily feel out of place in the center of a room, whereas a more angular couch may create an awkward flow. If you think this type of sectional might be your vibe, we'd use the curvaceous seating arrangements in Chrissy Teigen and John Legend's home designed by AD100 designer Jake Arnold as your style inspiration.

Modular Sectional: We consider modular sectionals to be the jack-of-all-trades of the seating world. With a modular arrangement the world is your oyster—want to add more seating to your L-shaped sectional by making it into a U? No problem. Not happy with a sectional all together? Lots of modular designs actually allow you to re-configure your furniture into single and loveseats. Think: Colman Domingo’s impressive Ligne Roset Togo configuration or the Mario Bellini velvet number in this Los Feliz home.

Sofa With Chaise: If you’re not completely sold on the idea of a sectional, a sofa chaise is the perfect middle ground. With this option, there’s no need to agonize over whether a left or right facing chaise works with your space—the detachable chaise allows you to switch it up.

What Features Should I Look for in the Best Sectional Sofas?

Determining the right size sectional for your space is key to a) getting it in the door and b) ensuring that the arrangement doesn’t overwhelm your living room. We would classify three size categories to help you narrow down which to make shopping a little easier on you:

Seat depth—or the distance between the backrest and the outer edge of the seat cushion—is another factor that you’ll want to consider for the ultimate comfort to match your height. There’s no right seat depth, per se, but a deeper-seated sofa is better suited for someone leggier or simply sprawling out, while something more narrow is ideal if you’re looking to sit more upright. Brands like Interior Define also custom make sectionals to your exact depth preference if you have a specific number in mind.

While we’d all like to champion the white couch lifestyle, it’s not always practical if you’re sharing a home with little ones or pets. Thankfully advancements in upholstery tech have developed performance fabrics that promise resistance to spills and durability against everyday wear and tear. You could easily add a luxurious feel to your space with a jewel-toned velvet à la John Legend and Chrissy Teigen or Vanessa Hudgens. But if you’re a traditionalist, you might find inspiration from neutral picks like Ashley Tisdale’s Sixpenny or Taylor Hill’s cloud sofa.

Lately, designers are demonstrating that statement sectionals are something to aspire to. One look at Kendall Jenner’s “grandma-chic” chintz sofa upholstered in Lee Jofa’s Hollyhock Handblock print, under the guidance of AD100 designer Heidi Callier, is an invitation to expand your own floral dreams. (Open Door viewers wouldn’t stop praising the bold design choice.)

A recent report on designers’ couch trend predictions for 2026 are generally pointing to a shift from blocky silhouettes to styles with rounded edges (à la Mario Bellini’s infamous Camaleonda sofa). These bulbous styles owe a lot to the popularity of conversation pits, encouraging banter between seated guests and a comfy, closed-in feel. Postmodern, relaxed silhouettes like the Natuzzi and slouchy Maralunga profiles are also enduringly relevant as cool personas of the sofa world.

When it comes to colorful choices, florals, plaids, and stripes are offered more frequently as ready-to-ship. People are also overwhelmingly gravitating to 1970s colorways and styles that are laid-back and comfy. But unlike something you’d find in an old wood-paneled basement, the upholstery is often applied to modern silhouettes.

#4786. Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#4783. Like Fine Wine, Life Can Improve With Age

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Aging reflects shared humanity; we are all in this together. Yet perceived purpose in life is a factor that we can improve. Research explores how to forge a positive path forward at any age.

Yiqing Yang and Kelin Li (2026) explored pathways to perceiving aging in older adults.[i] They acknowledge that self-perceptions of aging (SPA), defined as personal experiences, beliefs, and evaluations of the aging process, predict behavioral health outcomes as people grow older. Encompassing both positive and negative assessments, SPAs include perceptions of purpose, growth, and resilience, as well as concerns about physical, mental, or social decline. Yang and Li note that people experience aging differently, some seeing a decline in energy or physical ability while others enjoy improved emotional regulation. Not surprisingly, they recognize SPA as a robust predictor of physical and mental health, cognitive functioning, health-related behavior, and longevity.

Studying a racially diverse sample of adults aged 65 and older, Yang and Li identified some positive and negative predictors of SPA. One of the most significant was purpose in life, which consistently predicted higher positive SPA and lower negative SPA, making it an essential psychological resource over time. They note that purpose in life may prompt both meaning and direction, supporting an adaptive interpretation of aging. Accordingly, purpose can be viewed as an accumulated asset that may help older adults see aging as continuous growth as opposed to inevitable decline. This reframing can also protect against what Yang and Li refer to as internalized age stereotypes through maintaining a forward-looking orientation, counteracting age-related loss or perceived constraints.

Yang and Li note that their results also emphasize the concept of SPA as multidimensional. Positive SPA was linked with psychological strengths such as life satisfaction, purpose, and self-esteem, as well as a robust social life and religious affiliation. They interpret these findings as suggesting that maintaining a favorable view of aging is developed through psychological well-being, meaningful social engagement, and a sense of belonging. They contrast these positive outcomes with negative SPA, which was linked with negative outcomes such as having a limited social network, perceived constraints, more health problems, and higher religiosity, indicating that negative perceptions of aging may be explained less by the lack of resources than by perceptions of restrictions, loss, and declining autonomy.

Yang and Li advise caution when interpreting their findings regarding religious involvement. They observe that religious affiliation produces social connection and identity benefits that bolster positive views about aging, although a higher degree of religiosity may suggest different coping styles and responses to stress or health challenges that are linked to negative SPA. They therefore acknowledge the importance of assessing multiple dimensions of individual religious involvement, as opposed to viewing spirituality as a single construct. This advice is consistent with the reality that different religions have different belief systems, including views of the afterlife, which will effect older people differently than their younger counterparts.

Celebrating purpose in life can promote adaptive attitudes about aging and mitigate negative self-perception. It is never too late to be thankful for your circumstances, including faith, family, and friends, as well as your ability to continue to grow emotionally and spiritually. By taking stock of your blessings, which include not only worldly wealth but wisdom, you can refresh and renew a sense of purpose in life, as well as health, happiness, and hope for the future.

[i] Yang, Yiqing, and Kelin Li. “Psychosocial Resources and Constraints: Distinct Pathways to Positive and Negative Self-Perceptions of Aging in Diverse Older Adults.” Clinical Gerontologist: The Journal of Aging and Mental Health, May 11, 2026.

#4782. $20K Nissan NX7 PHEV goes on sale with nearly 200 miles of electric range

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its new NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

When the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The company’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The new NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Why is this article written like it will be available in the US market? It’s made in China and has Chinese software, we’ll never see it

The final production version will be shown to the public for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show later this month, but you can let us know what you think of the new NX7 in the comments, today.

#4781. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

#4779. Where Does Caroline Kennedy Live Now? Unpacking the Former First Daughter’s Real Estate Portfolio

She entered the public eye as a little girl living in the White House, but where does Caroline Kennedy live now? The only surviving child of President John F. Kennedy and Jacqueline Kennedy, the diplomat and author has lived in many prominent homes throughout her life, the Executive Mansion being just one of them. Below, we’re unpacking all of the places that Caroline has called home.

An aerial view of the Kennedy Compound in Hyannisport, Massachusetts

In 1956, the year before Caroline was born, her parents paid $45,948 for a home at the Kennedy Compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts, where JFK’s parents and brother, Robert F. Kennedy, also owned homes. The 4,500-square-foot residence was built in the mid-20s, which is also the period when the famed family first put roots in the area. Born on November 27, 1957, Caroline spent childhood summers at the Cape Cod enclave. It was also where, on July 19, 1986, she married museum exhibit designer Ed Schlossberg.

Caroline Kennedy and Edwin Schlossberg on their wedding day in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts

When Jacqueline died in 1994, the property went to Caroline and her brother, John F. Kennedy, Jr., but reportedly, only John spent his summers there. After he and his wife, Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, tragically died in a 1999 plane crash, the home’s ownership went to Caroline and her children. In 2004, Caroline sold the dwelling to her uncle, Senator Edward Kennedy, for $3 million. “It was sold to the senator to keep it in the family,” family friend Dick Gallagher told the Cape Cod Times. “It will always be the president’s house.”

Caroline spent her first few years primarily living in Washington, DC’s Georgetown neighborhood. In late 1957, her parents paid $82,000 for a brick Federal-style home and tapped designer Sister Parish to decorate its interiors. The Kennedys lived at the circa 1811 property, known as the William Marbury House for the Federalist financier who first lived there, until JFK’s 1961 presidential inauguration. John Jr. was also born during this period. The 5,215-square-foot residence was most recently sold in May 2026 for $6.125 million.

US President John F Kennedy in the Oval Office of the White House with John Kennedy Jr and Caroline Kennedy in 1962

Of course, the next residence that the Kennedys took up was the White House, where they lived from 1961 until President Kennedy’s 1963 assassination. Caroline attended kindergarten in the White House’s solarium along with about 20 other children. She was photographed riding her pony named Macaroni, a gift from Lyndon B. Johnson, on the White House lawn for Life magazine in 1962. The image inspired Neil Diamond to write his hit song, Sweet Caroline. In 2011, Caroline recalled celebrating childhood Halloweens in America’s most famous dwelling: “One of my favorite memories of living here is dressing up in my witch costume and going over to scare my father in his office,” she said.

After JFK’s death, Jacqueline, Caroline, and John moved back to Georgetown, in a $175,000 home known as the Newton D. Baker House, on the same street as their former home in the neighborhood. After less than a year of being hounded by tour buses at the residence, Jackie put the 1794-built Federal-style dwelling up for sale and headed for the Big Apple.

Jackie Kennedy Onassis outside of her 1040 Fifth Avenue home

The family of three moved into a 14-room penthouse apartment on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, which Jacqueline bought in July 1964 for $200,000. The 5,300-square-foot home had five bedrooms, five-and-a-half baths, and views of Central Park and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where Caroline later worked and met her future husband. The 18-story limestone building was built in 1930 by prominent architect Rosario Candela. The penthouse unit had a library, conservatory, three fireplaces, and a balcony overlooking the park. Caroline lived there until 1972, when she left to attend a boarding school in Massachusetts. Jacqueline called the apartment home until her 1994 death. A year later, billionaire David Koch bought the unit for $9.5 million.

An aerial view of Jackie Kennedy’s Martha’s Vineyard property

In 1979, Jacqueline bought Red Gate Farm, a 340-acre property on Martha’s Vineyard, for $1.1 million. At the time, only a small hunting cabin sat on the grounds. The former First Lady soon built an impressive compound comprised of a Cape Cod–style main house with five bedrooms, a four-bedroom guesthouse, a three-bedroom caretaker’s house, a boathouse, a storage building, two garages, a pool, a tennis court, and a treehouse for her grandchildren.

The property stayed in the family long after Jacqueline’s death. Caroline and Schlossberg’s daughter, Tatiana, was married at the residence in 2017. Two years later, Caroline listed Red Gate Farm for $65 million. “Forty years ago, my mother fell in love with Martha’s Vineyard. When she found Red Gate Farm, it was a perfect expression of her romantic and adventurous spirit,” she said in a statement. “The dunes and ponds and rolling hills of Aquinnah gave her the chance to create a world where she could be so close to nature, close to her family and friends, and, most importantly, close to her beloved books.”

In a letter printed in The Vineyard Gazette, Caroline explained her rationale for the sale. “Being able to raise our children in a place that meant so much to my mother and my brother has kept them close to our hearts. Now that our children are grown, it is time for them to spread their wings, and for us to explore new places.” The diplomat also recalled her pleasant memories at the property over the years: “Together we wove the traditions of summer across three generations — setting lobster pots in Menemsha Pond, entering the Fair and never winning, growing a vegetable garden, bringing home the best shell from the beach every day, getting stuck at the airport when the fog rolled in.”

In 2020, 304 acres of the property sold for $27 million to two nonprofits: the Martha’s Vineyard Land Bank Commission and the Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation. In 2025, it opened to the public as the Squibnocket Pond Reservation. A year later, the Land Bank Commission paid an additional $10 million for a 32-acre portion.

Caroline and Schlossberg still own 95 acres of the property, including the main house and guesthouse.

Caroline and Schlossberg primarily raised their children, Rose, Tatiana, and Jack, in an apartment on Park Avenue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. The dwelling has six rooms and was described in a 2009 NBC News report as “a low-key place covered with books and decorated with slip-covered sofas.” The couple seems to still own the residence.

Following Tatiana’s tragic death to cancer in June 2026, Jack told People that his parents had moved in with Tatiana’s husband to help take care of their grandchildren, aged two and four years old. “My parents are grandparents, but they’re really playing the role of new parents right now,” Jack told the outlet. “They live with my niece and nephew and take care of them every single day… they’re all living in the same apartment.” Three months before her death, Tatiana and her husband bought an Upper East Side co-op unit near her parents’ apartment.

#4778. Men of Pause: Redefining Manhood Through Vasectomy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

December 2014. She had just come out of an emergency C-section with our daughter. She was still shaking on the recovery table. She looked at me and said: “I'm done.”

She wasn't asking. She wasn't pushing me. She was just done.

September 2019. Galit needed to replace her IUD. This time, for the first time, we actually had an open discussion about it. Why does she need to take sole responsibility for birth control for both of us? I started considering a vasectomy. But I was scared. Not of the procedure. Scared of what it meant. Scared to close that chapter. Scared to end the part of me that was still, biologically, a man with options.

We researched, met a urologist, but ultimately, at the last minute, I bailed. Galit was happy that at least we spoke about it openly.

February 2026. I finally had my vasectomy.

The first time someone cut that part of my body, I was eight days old. I didn't choose it. I was ushered into a covenant, a tradition. This happened before I could speak, before I could consent, before I even knew I had a body.

That is how it goes for most men. The first major act performed on our reproductive organ happens without our permission. We enter the tribe like everyone else. Unaware. Another boy marked into the tribe.

For many of us, that pattern continues. Sex gets socialized into us as performance, as conquest, as something we take. Reproduction becomes the measure of our masculinity. Our job is to spread our seed. We are procreators. That is our identity. So when the vasectomy conversation comes up, most men hear one thing: Loss. That’s how I felt back then.

I want to suggest the opposite: A vasectomy doesn’t hurt your masculinity, it actually liberates you.

Some men hear the word vasectomy and their stomach tightens. It sounds like castration. Like a punishment.

I understand that feeling. Anything that touches that part of us is triggering. That part is the symbol for what we learn is our worth, our trophy, our uniqueness. Limiting or “damaging” it threatens our sense of manhood.

But this is different. This time you have agency. This is a choice you make. You decide what happens to your body. Not your parents. Not your religion.

In a way, vasectomy is a form of positive liberty. The first circumcision wasn’t your choice. Someone chose for you. The second one was made of your free choice. You choose it because you want to.

Isaiah Berlin called this positive liberty. By choosing the second cut, you gain the (positive) freedom to live your life according to your values.

Here’s what I didn’t expect. It’s been about 9 months since the operation and nothing has changed. Not physically. Not sexually. Not sensually. To be honest, my body feels like the procedure never happened.

The only thing that changed is how I see myself.

It was a symbolic circumcision. A symbolic change.

Maybe I'm entering another tribe now. A tribe of older men who are ready to initiate others, because it is no longer about me.

This is the threshold we wrote about in the relational hero's journey. Once he crosses the point of no return, he embarks on a journey, which will change him forever. He will return ‘home’, a wiser hero, bringing his new wisdom and abilities to change the world.

This is also what middle age has been teaching me. The focus shifts. From spreading the seed to serving others. From building my own life to initiating the men coming up behind me. Guiding men into mature, differentiated manhood. The books Iron John and The New Manhood teach us that the older man's task is not to keep proving himself. It is to initiate the younger ones. To age and to sage. A vasectomy, for me, was one way of stepping into that.

I call this being a man of pause. To pause, reflect, and take the time to care for others.

There is a principle screenwriting teacher Robert McKee returns to. The artist becomes more creative inside their limitation not outside it. I have felt this everywhere. Writing a PhD inside its rules. Training for a marathon within the plan. Learning to touch my wife the way she wants in a 30-day challenge. The limit is what helped me be better.

The vasectomy is a creative limitation. I blocked one dimension of my sexuality, the reproductive one, and what I got back was focus. Energy that is no longer worried about an unwanted pregnancy. Energy I can channel somewhere else. Toward my marriage, my art, my clinical work. Toward changing the world in the years I have left.

We fixate on what we will not be able to do anymore. The better question is what this limitation will open up? When you close the door on your reproduction, what new vista will appear?

I am not telling you to get a vasectomy. That is between you and your partner. I am asking you something else. I'm asking you to ask yourself:

Where in your life are you willing to cut something off?

Where do you dare to block one dimension of you, so you can evolve into the next version of yourself?

Where and how are you ready to evolve your manhood?

If men stopped thinking about themselves, put their ego aside, and turned toward service, that would change the world.

When you were a baby, someone made that choice for you.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D.-candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

Berlin, I. (1969). Two concepts of liberty. In Four essays on liberty (pp. 118–172). Oxford University Press.

Biddulph, S. (2014). The new manhood. Finch Publishing.

Bly, R. (1990). Iron John: A book about men. Addison-Wesley.

McKee, R. (1997). Story: Substance, structure, style, and the principles of screenwriting. ReganBooks.

#4777. High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

#4775. Mowing milestone: Greenzie surpasses 255,000 autonomous miles mowed

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie announced the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

#4773. Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”

On Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

As we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

The memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

That’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

#4772. The Overlooked Social Origins of Machiavellian Behavior

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 26, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

In 1532, statesman Niccolo Machiavelli's book The Prince was published across Renaissance Italy. While controversial, his magnum opus on statecraft was widely deemed innovative for de-emphasizing ethical norms and ultra-pragmatically explaining what leaders should do to hold and gain power.

Many philosophers before and after Machiavelli emphasized people as having a self-interested nature. Like him, they often emerged from ceaselessly unstable, war-prone milieus. Legalists from ancient China viewed Confucians as too morally idealistic; early modern England's Thomas Hobbes held a dimmer view of human nature than did John Locke. Yet, it was the term "Machiavellian" that endured and evolved in English writing since the mid-1500s. Today, it refers to being calculated, insincere, and even unprincipled to gain something.

As a psychological concept, "Machiavellianism" is associated with cynical, manipulative, and self-serving tendencies. Psychologists have even measured it through scales like the MACH-IV and Five-Factor Machiavellianism Inventory. Popular articles and videos abound with titles about how to find "narcissists" among partners, or to beware of "dark triad" traits in co-workers. Whether or not they capture phenomenologically valid constructs, or align with how health professionals use these terms, they do not always include structural approaches and takeaways. Could how Machiavellianism presents in societies give clues into broader social issues needing addressing?

People with similar childhood adversities can grow up to have very different worldviews. However, for some, a combination of early deprivations, caregiver modeling, and hereditary factors can increase their likelihood of internalizing cynical outlooks. These could crystallize into enduring, Machiavellian patterns of interaction later on. Early childhood attachment disruptions, relational losses, and conditional, inconsistent affection can contribute to understanding relationships as ultimately transactional. Frequent bullying, abuse, or social injustices without accountability might misguide some to view ethical and, sometimes, institutional rules as naive or frivolous.

Later, resulting cravings for "omnipotent control" can lead to great efforts to control how most others view and treat oneself, sometimes in ways contradictory to one's actual self. One applies an astute "theory of mind" for envisioning what others want. Consider a group leader who speaks frequently of uplifting and bringing people together, but privately gossips and plays potential competitors against each other. Or a colleague who cultivates a reputation as a light-hearted jokester, but emotionally abuses their partner at home. Their friends might not believe they have such dissonant traits, let alone have suspected these early on. Indeed, psychoanalysts refer to the superego lacunae of otherwise upstanding people who harbor deeply dark tendencies in specific domains of life.

But how useful is it, really, to focus on the sensationalism, the individual "wrongness" or "pathology," or the developmental roots of Machiavellian characteristics? Nobody denies that manipulation and relational aggression happen. Individuals with such traits--or at least a strong disposition to them--exist in all human societies, but how and to what extent these manifest depends greatly on one's present and future environments.

Historian E.P. Thompson examined the moral economy of everyday Englishmen in the 1700s, focusing on nuanced motivations of bread riots beyond hunger itself. As Thompson's work supported, people may be at least as driven to drastic action--in his examples, selective intimidation and aggression toward middlemen--by perceived violations of what is normatively reasonable and fair, than by economic inequality in and of itself.

Yet, unlike for his early modern examples, vigilante retribution is no longer as tolerated in most societies. "Fighting fire [i.e. injustices] with fire" can nowadays land people in prison, depending on their methods. Cynicism may then simmer if people see widespread violation of implicit norms of fairness without meaningful consequences.

Examples appear painfully difficult for the observer to challenge; they range from deliberate decisions, like leaders' rewarding betrayals of colleagues who find themselves in hard times, to rigidly structural imbalances like co-workers getting overlooked for opportunities due to their ethnicity, gender, or religion. In turn, self-serving, insincere, performative, and manipulative behaviors can become gradually more tolerated, rewarded, and normalized in groups. Generalized trust, authenticity, good-faith charity, and optimism might all slowly wither.

Is it useful to think of widespread Machiavellianism as mutually reinforcing and cyclically associated with greater cynicism in a society? Maybe yes, but that is also not the full picture. Perhaps in most cases, prone to quid pro quo exchanges and transactional alliance-building, Machiavellianism is unlikely to improve social issues long-term. It would not benefit any group's already low-trust culture, declining public confidence in a given institution, or corruption. If anything, the rewarding of one's playing dirty could encourage more of such tendencies in their circles via social learning.

Yet, for some others, witnessing Machiavellianism's normalization might not transform their personalities overall. It would instead outwardly modify their interpersonal approaches to achieving pre-existing, potentially socially constructive goals. These ends, regardless of their means, go beyond everyday self-preservation and range from improving the marginalized social status of one's group to advancing a specific policy.

What might such Machiavellian-like adaptation or imitation look like for someone who did not grow up with overtly congruent traits? Examples include adopting more guardedness and suspicion, calculation and self-restraint in what one says and to whom, flattery, selectively concealing one's true feelings, and discreetly discerning colleagues' interests and "agendas." Saying things one does not fully mean or feel may seem advantageous, even encouraged, when one assumes their superiors do the same. One might increasingly rationalize their strategic exploitation of others' misfortunes. If these are the prevailing, implicit rules of engagement in one's organizational or workplace politics, then so they will practice them. As with what Friedrich Nietzsche said about fighting monsters, they should also take care lest they essentially "become" Machiavellian through and through.

Not every instance of Machiavellianism in one's workplace, organization, or community indicates a structurally sick society. A few individuals, regardless of how much privilege they have, can still demonstrate such features during periods of widespread optimism and trust, even if their tendencies are more the exception than the norm. Conversely, not everyone who has developed a protective cynicism wants to take advantage of others.

That said, how prevalent Machiavellianism is in a group at a given time may hint at underlying competition over resources perceived as both finite and unfairly allocated. Resources are not necessarily just material wealth, but also social capital, status, and power. Underhanded ways of interaction may reflect not just neurodevelopmental predispositions but also, for those who are most angry, disillusioned, or hardened, an instrumental means of efficiently accumulating such resources.

None of this absolves the need for accountability and responsibility for inflicting interpersonal harms. Advocacy can be done primarily through good-faith methods. Leaders can promote workplace cultures that are more fair and transparent than what they knew in the past. Yet, so long as racism, sexism, xenophobia, homophobia, and other social ills persist, Machiavellianism may continue to appear to some a legitimate way of navigating work and life--not just for those seeking to maintain great privilege, but also, and perhaps especially, for many people without much of it.

#4771. Volkswagen prices its new ID. Cross for the UK, but the $35,000 version comes later

Volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.

After opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.

The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

Following the ID. Polo, the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

When the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

The ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen said the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.

All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.

Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.

Volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.

The base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

Volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

As the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”

Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the new ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.
